speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND THE EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-20, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill implements the changes announced in the Budget of April 27, 1989, concerning excise taxes and duties on tobacco products and gasoline, and increases in sales tax rates pending the implementation of the goods and services tax. These measures reflect our commitment to deal with the problem of our substantial and increasing national debt. Meeting this challenge and meeting it successfully is a responsibility that we have to present and future generations of Canadians.
During the past four years, we have acted to restrain public spending. We have closed tax loopholes for business and high-income individuals. These measures have reduced the annual deficit and slowed the growth of the debt. Additional measures are needed, however, to ensure that the national debt does not jeopardize our ability to maintain programs valued by Canadians and to sustain the economic growth and high standard of living they expect to enjoy.
The measures taken in this Budget to control the debt affect government spending and revenues. They were carefully chosen to ensure a balanced approach that takes regional situations into account and that imposes the heaviest burden on those who are most able to bear it. The revenue measures are also distributed in a balanced way among several categories, including the federal sales tax and excise duties and taxes.
The federal sales tax is also the centrepiece of another key element of our strategy to strengthen Canada's economy and preserve essential programs. The present sales tax will be replaced by the new goods and services tax on January 1, 1991. The new tax will provide a more stable foundation for dealing with the public debt problem. It will improve the overall fairness of the tax system. It will make federal sales taxes more visible to consumers. Finally, and most important, it will result in significant gains for economic production in all sectors of the economy and all regions of Canada.

One of the key elements of the Bill we are considering today is an across-the-board increase in the existing federal sales tax rates in advance of federal sales tax reform.
Some Hon. Members may question why the Government would raise the tax rates under the current federal sales tax system at this time, when it is widely recognized as being seriously flawed. These rate increases provide a revenue bridge to the new goods and services tax. They will provide much needed revenue to address the deficit and debt problems pending sales tax reform, while avoiding more substantial increases in other taxes, in particular personal income tax. Given the major deficiencies of the manufacturer's sales tax, it is only possible to use the existing system to help meet the Government's fiscal needs now, because it will be replaced in a little over 18 months. The relatively short time that the system will remain in place will minimize the incentive for business to engage in the tax planning and avoidance activities that have helped undermine it.
Moreover, the problems associated with the current system will not be seriously compounded by the rate increases because of the brief period during which the rate increases will apply.
The rate increases include a 1.5 per cent increase in the general sales tax rate from 12 per cent to 13.5 per
June 6, 1989

cent, effective June 1,1989. The other sales tax rates will all be increased by 1 per cent to 19 per cent for alcohol and tobacco products, effective April 28, 1989; 11 per cent for telecommunication and telecommunication programming services, effective June 1, 1989; and to 9 per cent for construction materials, effective Januaiy 1,1990. Together, these measures will contribute about $1 billion in 1989 and $2 billion in 1990 toward reducing the deficit.
It is the policy of this Government to provide assistance through the tax system to help those in need. In the February, 1986 Budget, the Government introduced the refundable sales tax credit to benefit low-income Canadians. With the implementation of the goods and services tax, we will be introducing a new sales tax credit which will involve a substantial expansion in current benefits. The new credit will ensure that families earning less than $30,000 per year will be better off as a result of sales tax reform.
In the interim, the existing sales tax credit is being doubled and the threshold increased in order to more than compensate recipients of the full credit for the sales tax rate increases. The budget Bill to implement changes in the Income Tax Act will increase the refundable sales tax credit for adults from $70 to $100 in 1989, and to $140 in 1990. For children under age 19, the credit will be increased from $35 to $50 in 1989, and to $70 in 1990. The income threshold for credit will be increased from $16,000 to $18,000 in 1990. Therefore, a two parent family with two children, and an income of up to $18,000 will receive a maximum credit of $420 in 1990.

To come back to the Bill that we are considering today, I would like to draw your attention to the changes implementing increased excise duties and taxes for tobacco products.
Under the Bill, excise duties on cigarettes, together with the federal sales tax, will increase the federal revenue from cigarettes by $4 a carton. The excise duty and tax on cigars increases proportionally. These measures should generate some $535 million in additional revenue in 1989 and $770 million in 1990.
The Bill provides two increases in excise duty and tax for manufactured tobacco. The first amounts to $4 per 200 grams and took effect on April 28, 1989. The second will add $1.30 per 200 grams to the sales and excise taxes and the excise duty and will take effect on October 1, 1989.
Excise Tax Act
As well as adding revenue to lighten the debt burden, the increased duty and taxes on manufactured tobacco will bring the rates on this product closer to those for cigarettes. The wide gap between them encourages consumption and development of manufactured tobacco products such as fine-cut tobacco which make it possible to avoid paying the higher duties and taxes on cigarettes. Thus, federal government revenues decreased as regular cigarette smokers turned to other tobacco products.
Mr. Speaker, these changes to tobacco taxes, in addition to providing the government with revenue it greatly needs, are part of its overall strategy to reduce tobacco use in Canada.

The Bill also implements increases in the excise taxes on gasoline and aviation gasoline. With these increases, excise taxes will rise by one cent per litre as of April 28, 1989, and by an additional one cent on January 1,1990, to generate $250 million in 1989 and $660 million in 1990.
As part of the changes in taxes on motive fuels, the excise tax on leaded gasoline is increased an additional one cent per litre, effective April 28,1989. This measure will help to accelerate the decline in the use of leaded fuel as we adjust to the phasing out of lead in gasoline by December 1, 1990.
Under the goods and services tax to be implemented on January 1, 1991, all commercial users will be entitled to recover federal sales tax on motor vehicle fuels used for business purposes. To provide a bridge to the new system, the sales tax portion of the fuel tax rebate program for farmers, fishermen and other primary producers, which is scheduled to expire on December 31, 1989, will be extended for one additional year. For the period after December 31, 1989, until the goods and services tax commences on January 1, 1991, farmers will continue to be eligible for a sales tax rebate of 3.5 cents per litre while other primary producers will receive sales tax rebates of three cents per litre on motive fuels used for off-highway production purposes.
Finally, this Bill contains a number of technical amendments. New marking requirements are being introduced in the Excise Act to address concerns that cigarettes are being imported illegally without payment of federal taxes and duties. Also, certain archaic provisions regarding the burden of proof in offences under the Excise Act are being amended. In the Excise Tax Act,

June 6, 1989
Excise Tax Act
the point of imposition of the tax on laundry detergent is being shifted from the manufacturer's level to the wholesale trade level to correct anomalies in the application of sales tax to these products.
In conclusion, I want to emphasize that this Bill is an important part of the responsive and responsible action plan to deal with the public debt, as set out in the Budget. It recognizes the need to build on our progress to date and to take firm action at this time to ensure that we can pass on to the next generation the ability to protect and strengthen the fundamental values that are so much a part of life in Canada.
Therefore, I urge the Hon. Members to give their full support to this Bill and to ensure that it is approved by this House as quickly as possible.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND THE EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister, in introducing his Bill this morning, has placed it squarely in the context of the Budget and the Budget's objectives in attempting to reduce the deficit costs which have mounted steadily since the Government took office almost five years ago.
The impact of continuing high rates of deficit spending and the demands of interest obligations on the debt has been such that the Governments attempting to counter those increases by major tax increases, less by government expenditure control and more by tax increases.
Here we have today the first tangible evidence of the Government's intention to move against its deficit by taxing Canadians in what is a regressive way. The Minister knows full well that the sales tax increase that he has proposed today, from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent, which will be in place as he pointed out for the next year and a half, is a regressive tax. It impacts more on the lower income Canadians than it does on the more affluent. It also continues a tax that by the Government's own recognition is what the Minister of Finance has called "a silent killer of jobs".
The manufacturers' sales tax is an outdated form of taxation. We have had it in place since 1924 when we were the first country to introduce such a tax. Today, we
are the only country still with a manufacturers' sales tax. The Government is now increasing that same sales tax, which it recognizes is regressive and which it recognizes is an outmoded form of taxation, from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent.
It is a sales tax which is largely hidden from consumers. It is concealed in the price of goods. It may well be that some Canadians will not be aware immediately of the impact of this regressive tax measure intended to reduce the size of the Government's deficit.
The manufacturers' sales tax, by the Government's own recognition, has another major problem. It impacts much more severely on Canadian exporters, Canadians attempting to export abroad, than it does on importers. Yet, the Government has gone ahead and increased that adverse impact even more than it has in the past.
The manufacturers' sales tax, in that sense and indeed in a variety of ways, distorts the production and distribution decisions of corporations. Most corporations, with any imagination, attempt to find ways of transferring the impact of the tax from manufacturing to the non-taxable part of their activities, that is, marketing and distribution. The result is a further distortion in the impact of the manufacturers' sales tax.
I would submit that in addition the manufacturers' sales tax which the Government is now increasing-not reducing, not eliminating, not replacing by any other tax, but rather seeking to increase it-is complicated in its administration. We have several levels of sales taxes in Canada, such as the manufacturers' sales tax and the excise taxes, which the Government is again increasing today. The effective tax rates for a number of items vary substantially, again causing distortions in our sales tax system.
I could go on for some time about the inadequacies and the distortions of the manufacturers' sales tax. I am sure the Minister will want to reply, if he has the occasion to do so, that the goods and services tax is intended to eliminate some of those problems.
However, the fact remains that today the Government is increasing from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent that same tax which it regards as unfair, inequitable, and distorting. We are expected today to accept that increase as a

sensible policy in the total government effort to reduce its deficit.
I would say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Minister, that this piece of legislation today confirms what Canadians have recognized, that is, that the Government of Canada, in attempting to reduce its deficit very late in the economic cycle, long after it should have taken corrective action if indeed it were serious about reducing its deficit, is doing so in a way that is regressive and impacts more on lower income Canadians than on the more affluent.
I said a moment ago that the Government has left it late in the economic cycle to take any corrective action with regard to the deficit. It is well recognized that the Government took no action from 1986, for whatever reasons; we can all speculate. My own view is that they were directly related to its standing in the public opinion polls at the time. From 1986 to 1988, it took no effective action on reducing the deficit.
Now, at this late stage in the economic cycle when a downturn is expected, we see the Government introducing a variety of measures in the name of deficit reduction, including an increase in the sales tax which may well have the impact-and this is a point I shall return to in a moment-of making the expected downturn even more severe than had hitherto been anticipated.
It is a traditional role of government that in prosperous times such as Canada has enjoyed for the last six or seven years, a Government acts to reduce its intervention in the economy and its spending and to put funds aside for what inevitably will be less prosperous times. This Government failed to do so. This Government has moved at the end of the economic cycle in a way that, as many independent economic forecasters and experts would have us understand, is more likely to create hardship in Canada than in fact rectify this Government's deficit problem.
I want to turn for a moment to the impact of this tax on the Canadian people. I have said that the increase in the manufacturers' sales tax is regressive, despite the fact that the Government had initially and indeed throughout its recent mandate taken the position that expenditure control was the primary focus of its fiscal management; not tax increases but expenditure control would be its chosen tool for deficit reduction.
Excise Tax Act
What we have in this Budget is a program of tax increases. Far more important in this Budget is the tax increase element rather than expenditure control. The result is that we have a Government that has not lived up to its promises of four or five years ago. We have not seen the Government carry out its commitment to ensure that taxes were reduced and not increased.
The net effect of the Government's actions in this Budget is to increase the tax burden on all Canadians further. In the case of sales taxes, taxes directly on the products which Canadians consume, we have had an increase in the sales tax rate from 9 per cent to 12 per cent during the previous mandate of this Government. That sales tax has now been increased again. Today the Minister is introducing a Bill increasing that same sales tax from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent. Thatof course must be added to a 10 per cent tax on long distance telephone calls, which has now become 11 per cent. There was already a 5-cent per litre increase in the gasoline tax, which has now become 7 cents per litre. For those of us who are affluent enough to travel by air, there has been an increase in air transport taxes without, it appears, any additional safety in the air.
The central question in any tax increase is whether they are fair or spread equitably among taxpayers. The Minister, the House, and Canadians know that sales taxes, whatever the credits the Government may wish to bring forward, are by their very nature inequitable. A sales tax is regressive. It will hurt lower income Canadians more than it will hurt more affluent Canadians. It is the opposite of a progressive income tax. A sales tax impacts inequitably. It impacts more on lower income Canadians.
The record of this Government in increasing inequitable and regressive taxes is deplorable. I could cite a number of instances. The National Council of Welfare, for example, recently demonstrated in a study that during the first four years of this Government's mandate, the personal income taxes of a working family went up by 60 per cent, those of a middle income family went up by 17 per cent, while those of an upper income family went down by 6 per cent. Those are personal income taxes, and of course it is a result of this Government's

June 6, 1989
Excise Tax Act
determination to deindex income tax, which it has done in previous Budgets and again in this one, and to impose a 3 per cent income surtax in the past which in this Budget now becomes 5 per cent.
The real increases in taxes during the past four years have not only been in income tax, but it has been in sales taxes. For example, the increase in the manufacturer's sales tax in the past from 9 per cent to 12 per cent. The combination of higher income taxes and higher sales taxes in the recent Budget means that an average income family will now pay $700 more in taxes annually. This means in turn that the average Canadian family is now paying $2,000 more in taxes since the Conservative Government was first elected in 1984.
With that piling of tax upon tax, of income tax upon income tax through the surtax, through the deindexing of income taxes, and through the increase in the manufacturer's sales tax and excise taxes today, no wonder we have heard nothing more from the Minister of Finance-about his 1984 election promise not to raise taxes. Here is another example of a Conservative Government that makes promises before a campaign, the 1984 promise to reduce taxes, but have had nothing but increases in taxes for the last five years.
Prior to the recent election, we had a series of promises totalling some $17 billion about the great measures the Government would undertake. The day after the election, however, the Government found surprisingly that its cupboard was bare and that it had to increase taxes in order to meet the demands of interest payments on its debt, a debt that has risen from approximately $170 billion when this Government took office to $350 billion today.
In this Bill we are talking about increases in the sales taxes and excise taxes. The $2 billion to be generated by the federal sales tax compares to total income tax increases of less than $1 billion. Quite obviously, this means that the Government is relying more on a regressive than a progressive form of taxation. A greater reliance by the Government on sales taxes rather than on income taxes to generate additional revenue means that the burden of taxation is being moved even more from high income earners to lower income Canadians who pay a greater proportion of their incomes in sales taxes.
Let us look at that matter for one moment. I want to draw the attention of the House and indeed of all Canadians to the fact that we as a result of a combination of income tax and sales taxes, taxes on families with children are being increased more than taxes on families without children. For a one income family, taxes on an average family with two children have gone up more than $900, compared to an average one income earner family without children. We see here a greater impact on Canadians families with children than those without.
The budget measures the Minister brought forward today, combined with other aspects of the Budget, means that total taxes on an average single parent family with two children have been increased over $250 since 1984. For a family with two children where both parents work, the total taxes paid by a family at the poverty line have almost tripled since this Government took office.
In contrast, total taxes paid by a family with two children where both parents work and earn more than $100,000 have increased only 11 per cent since 1984. In other words, the taxes of a family near the poverty line, with two children, and both parents working, have gone up 176 per cent, whereas the taxes of a comparable family with $100,000 or more of income have gone up only 11 per cent. If that is progressive and fair taxation, it is not my definition.

When the budget measures are fully implemented,as I gather is the intention of the Government, the additional tax burden borne by Canadians will be increased by an average of $382 per family-$151 in personal taxes and $231 in the type of consumption tax which the Minister is bringing forward today. Of the 10 million families in Canada, 8.3 million will see their after tax income drop as a result of this Budget. The Budget impacts most severely on two parent families with children. I have already pointed out the impact on them. The sales taxes which the Minister has introduced today will have an especially adverse impact on families, an intent that this Government denies but
June 6, 1989

has nevertheless given constant expression to during its previous mandate and during the course of this mandate.
I want to turn to the question of regional considerations of a federal sales tax change. The Minister will recognize that the regions of Canada, those distant from the principal areas of production and distribution in our country, incur higher taxes and pay a higher part of a sales tax than those Canadians living in what is called central Canada, near or at the places of manufacture and production.
The costs of shipping goods to the more remote regions is embedded in the final price of those goods. Therefore, when the Minister imposes higher transport costs as a result of the increases in fuel taxes, the basic price of goods, and hence the sales tax paid on them, will be higher in remote regions. People living in more remote regions will pay more sales tax than those living in central Canada. The tax credits available, which the Minister extolled in his speech this morning, make no allowance for regional considerations. The adverse impact on Canadians living in the regions are greater than on those in central Canada. There is no offset, no credit, no effort on the part of this Government to compensate those in the regions for the fact that they must pay higher taxes.
This is from the same Government that in a variety of ways has imposed a severe burden on the regions. A greater burden as a result of this Budget has been imposed on the regions than has been imposed on what has been called central Canada. I say that because we are all conscious of the fact that the reduction by this Government of transfer payments to the provinces, the way in which it introduced the tax-back of old age pensions and of family allowances, has the indirect result of reducing further the tax revenues of the provinces.
The closing of military bases, the changes in the way in which UIC will be provided for those in high unemployment areas combine to have a major impact on the regions. Today we have yet another piece of legislation, namely, the increase in the excise and sales taxes, which will only exacerbate the already severe impact of this Budget on the regions.
Excise Tax Act
I want to turn for a moment to the question of the inflationary impact of sales taxes. The Minister knows, the House knows and the Canadian people know that sales taxes are by their very nature not only regressive but inflationary. They increase the cost of goods and services. Increased prices drive up inflation. They are an expression of inflation within our country. What we have then today is a situation which as a result of this Budget will make yet more serious the possibilities, not only of economic recession as I mentioned a moment ago but of higher inflation. Indirect taxes are one cause of higher inflation.
I am sorry that the Minister has chosen to leave the House and not continue to participate in the discussion.

I was saying that the indirect tax increases embodied in this Budget will cause higher inflation, so the dilemma facing this Government has not really addressed.
The risk of inflation is enhanced, leaving Canadians without any prospect of significant cuts in interest rates. On the contrary, the indirect tax measures which the Minister has introduced today, and indeed the goods and services tax which the Government intends to become effective January 1, 1991, will fuel inflation. The increases certainly will not encourage the Governor of the Bank of Canada to lower interest rates in what he sees as his fight against inflation. Indeed, the direct result of the sales tax increases will put upward pressure on interest rates.
Many in the business community in particular are concerned that this Budget, by choosing the tax route and not the expenditure control route, has not given room for a more accommodative monetary policy by the Bank of Canada. Therefore, in those circumstances we can be quite certain that we will see, partly as a result of these major sales tax increases, a further increase in interest rates or at least a continuation of the present

June 6, 1989
Excise Tax Act
high level of real interest rates in Canada and a major difference in those rates between U.S. and Canada.
This Government has in the past got wrong its mix of high interest rate policy and high deficit spending. Those two policies combine to make life more difficult for all Canadians in the sense that higher interest rates drive up the cost of the deficit, and the Government then imposes higher sales taxes to pay for those higher interest rates. However, in so doing the Government drives up inflation. The bank says "well, we must now have higher interest rates to counter that inflation". We are into a vicious circle, and this Budget and the sales tax measures brought before us today only make that vicious circle yet more difficult.
Real interest rates are simply too high. They are now at a level where they themselves contribute to inflationary pressures. It is not surprising that the Conference Board of Canada, one of the more respected of the economic institutions in our country, has noted that the Budget is disappointing on the one hand to the financial and business communities that were expecting larger expenditure cuts and, on the other hand, is damaging to consumers who were hard hit with tax increases.
The Conference Board has raised the very real question of whether the present mix of high interest rates and high government spending is right. It has raised the question of whether this Budget, even late in the economic cycle, has addressed that central problem.
The Government acts as if it had nothing to do with interest rates, that it is something to do with a man along Wellington Street at the Bank of Canada. That of course is nonsense. The Government has pursued the high interest rate policies. It fully agreed with the Governor of the Bank of Canada in imposing high interest rates, higher than they have been in the past five years.
There is little evidence that the pursuit of that high interest rate policy during the past two years is in fact countering inflationary pressures. Certainly the Government is doing nothing to offset this unequal regional impact of high interest rates.
I spoke a few moments ago about the fact that sales tax increases and the Budget generally have a particularly harsh impact on the regions. High interest rate policies, of course, have yet a further harsh impact on the regions.
The inflation which the Governor of the Bank of Canada so fears is generated largely by central Canada. The Government and the Governor of the Bank insist on pursuing their high interest rate policies in an effort to stifle what they see as the inflationary pressures coming out of central Canada, but the only way that they can compensate the regions is by introducing fiscal measures for regional development that will offset that adverse impact of the monetary policy.
However, what do we see in the Budget? In fact, we see a net reduction in the transfers to the provinces and to the regions, not an increase in the amount of transfers to help the regions counter the adverse impact of higher interest rates.
The further result of the high interest rate policies that this Government has pursued, and gives every reason to believe will be further pursued in light of the inflationary impacts of this Budget and of the sales tax increases, is that we have been attracting U.S. dollars into Canada which seek a higher rate of return than they would receive domestically. The result is that the value of the Canadian dollar has been driven up.
A further result is that Canadian exporters encounter yet more and more difficulty in pursuing their export opportunities in the United States and elsewhere. So we have a further result of high interest rates, which is that Canadian exports have been adversely impacted.
A third problem with high interest rates and high Government borrowing is that generally affluent people benefit from that borrowing. It is higher income people who have the money to lend to the Government, yet it is all Canadian taxpayers who have to pay for that Government borrowing. They have to pay for the interest on the Government borrowing. The net result of that is that we get sales tax increases today. In part, we are getting sales tax increases so that Government has some additional revenue to pay for the interest on the money that it borrows from more affluent Canadians, the rentiers, if you wish, of Canada.
The net social impact of all this is simple. It is a transfer of money from poorer Canadians, lower income Canadians , less affluent Canadians who are paying a disproportionate amount of the sales tax to help repay the higher income Canadians who lend their money to the Government to help the Government meet its debt obligations. It will be clear from what I have said that I
June 6, 1989

am very much convinced that the current mix of monetary policies, high interest rates and fiscal policy, because of its undue reliance on monetary restraint, has adverse implications for our economy, for unemployment, which the Government itself acknowledges is going to increase as a result of this Budget; for the regional disparities that I have mentioned; for investment levels and hence on greater productivity which Canada needs in a more global trading economy.
I have perhaps said enough to indicate that we on this side of the House are not much enamoured of these excise tax increases which the Government has brought forward in its Bill today. They have a severe impact on lower income Canadians that will not be offset by any credit that the Minister wishes to introduce.
Sales taxes are regressive. They have an adverse impact on those who can least afford to pay them. We see also that regional disparities are increased as a result of this Budget. Inflationary pressures will be further increased as a result of the measures which the Minister has introduced today and will be further stimulated by the goods and services tax which the Government intends to put in place in 18 months.
It will come as no surprise to you, Mr. Speaker, that on this side of the House, we shall oppose and oppose vigorously, this Bill which does nothing to rectify the errors and the disadvantages of the existing sales tax. It only makes those problems worse by increasing the level of the tax. Its worst feature of all is its impact on lower-income families who will not receive adequate compensation for the impact of this tax.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND THE EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are debating Bill C-20 at the second reading stage. I think there has been a mistake on the Bill itself because the title says this is an Act to amend the Excise Thx Act and the Excise Act. Perhaps the title ought to have read that this is the largest tax grab in Canadian history. That would be a more accurate reflection as to what we are debating today.
Excise Tax Act
The topics put on these Bills sound rather innocuous. It says, "An Act to Amend the Excise Tkx Act and the Excise Act". When one hears that, it does not sound too bad. One thinks that this is something that Governments do. It has to amend these Acts from time to time.
When we actually get into it and starts analyzing what all this legislative gobbledegook actually says, it says that the Government has decided to reach into the pocket books, wallets and purses of Canadians like we have never experienced in the entire history of our country before. This is the most massive tax grab we have ever seen. It goes beyond everything people ever imagined.
I do not recall during the last election campaign when the Members from Prince George-Peace River, or from Lanark-Carleton were out on the hustings describing a plan to have this incredible tax grab occur if they were elected.
The Hon. Member was in Kamloops. I remember his visit well. I cannot recall press reports that said the Hon. Minister of State for Forests was going to be planning this massive tax grab if the Conservatives were elected. As a matter of fact, I do not recall even a mention of increased taxes.
Perhaps we should not even be discussing this Bill C-20 today. As a matter of fact, there is a better reason that we should not even be discussing Bill C-20 today. That is because this whole process is illegitimate. The Government should never have introduced its Budget from which this particular Bill flows because of the way it was handled.
It is the only time in parliamentary history in the face of the earth where a Government has leaked out a Budget days in advance and says that that is just the way it is and there is nothing one can do about it. It says that this is the way we do business here.
It is the only time in world history where a parliamentary system has seen a Minister of Finance who has ample evidence his Budget has been leaked, and knows that many people in privileged positions have had advance copies of the Budget, yet says that that is just the way it is and we are not going to do anything about that. Then he continues on with the Budget, reading it on television.

June 6, 1989
Excise Tax Act
I think we have to look long and hard in the annals of history to find a Minister of Finance that introduced a Budget via press conference the day before the scheduled presentation in the House of Commons.
We consider the Budget itself to be illegitimate. We ought to be considering Bill C-20 to be an illegitimate piece of legislation before the House.
This Government has decided to ignore all of the advice that has been given. It has decided to ignore every reflection that Canadians have been able to provide the Government and every editorial writer of financial affairs saying that the Minister should resign and start over. It just sort of blunders on, regardless of the people.
In the last few days, we have been reminded of another Government in another part of the world that has done a similar sort of thing in terms of attitude: forget the people. " We know what is best". Father Knows Best. Remember that old television program? The Government says it knows what is best for Canadians. It is going to impose this incredible tax grab at this very critical time for the people of Canada. What is this going to do to our country?
The justification of the Minister was that something had to be done about this deficit problem. We all agree.
Once again my memory fails me because I do not recall the Minister of Finance or the government Members who were running the last federal election making a big to-do about the deficit and indicating how to reduce it. Now we are finding out. We are finding out the real agenda, because rather than do it in a fair, just and equitable way, there will be a continuation of this regressive path of increasing sales and excise taxes on ordinary working people.
There is another way, as we are well aware. That other way is to start collecting a few taxes from some of the large profitable corporations that do not pay anything. Those people listening and watching today just do not believe that there are thousands of large, profitable corporations that fail to pay one penny in income tax year after year. People do not believe it because it sounds too ridiculous and incredible. Yet I have here the Minister of Finance's own statements where he identifies a number of profitable corporations that do not pay any income tax. There are more than 60,000 profitable corporations that exist in Canada that do not pay a penny in income tax. That is to say nothing of the thousands
that may pay 50 cents or $20 in income tax. This is a list of the ones that do not pay anything.
They are not the small Mom and Pop shops, the auto-body shop at the comer, or the hair salon down the street. They are companies such as Alcan of Canada that made a profit of $312 million in 1986-87 and did not pay one penny in income tax. There are others such as Hees International, Cadillac-Fairview, and Trilon Financial. There are 60,000 that do not pay any income tax at all.
Why would the Government on the one hand state that we have to struggle against this deficit yet fail to take an obvious course of action? For example, in 1986 the United States administration stated that it was unreasonable, unjust, unfair and discriminatory to allow large corporations to pay no income tax, so it introduced a minimum corporate tax. I give the United States credit for that. Now those corporations that are able to take advantage of the dozens and dozens of loopholes that are listed in the Government's handbooks still have to pay at least a minimum corporate tax. Does the Conservative Government in Canada follow suit in a fair and equitable manner? No, that is not in the cards. There is a better way. Let's get ordinary people again. Let's pass more of the tax burden to ordinary men and women.
In 1950 we had a tax system that was essentially balanced. The revenues coming in from people and the revenues coming in from the corporate sector were relatively balanced at 50-50. With all due respect to the Liberal finance critic who has just spoken, over the years as a result of successive Liberal and Conservative Governments this 50-50 balance has now shifted to 85 per cent of the revenues coming from people and less than 15 per cent coming from the corporate sector. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it a fair system when 85 per cent of the revenues come from people and only 15 per cent come from the corporate sector?
It does not matter whether a Liberal or a Conservative Government is in power. As a matter of fact, I believe the present Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) when he was Minister of Finance in a previous Liberal Government, introduced this whole myriad of corporate loopholes that resulted in 100,000 profitable corporations in those days, not 60,000, that paid no income tax. The Tories have moved to close off the most ludicrous loopholes and have got it down to only 60,000
June 6, 1989

large, profitable corporations that manage not to pay any income tax year after year.
What else could be done? If we are concerned about the deficit, which we are, let us take some real action and introduce a tax system that treats the various sectors of the economy in a fair and just manner. Who pays income tax in the business sector? Small and medium-sized businesses are paying more than they should because the large corporate taxpayers are getting away scot-free in many cases.
There is another issue and that is the whole matter of the interest rate policy. I am sure when you read all the newspapers this morning, Mr. Speaker, you also noticed that the Americans have reduced their interest rates. Now their interest rates are 2.5 per cent lower than ours in Canada. When one crosses the border there is an extreme variation in interest rates. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what the difference would be in our country if the Minister of Finance came into the Elouse this afternoon and made a statement that tomorrow morning interest rates in Canada will be reduced 2.5 per cent to harmonize with those in the United States.
Two things would happen immediately. It would send a clear signal to those people in the country who want to expand their operations, purchase new goods or supplies, or new services. With interest rates 2.5 per cent lower many economic initiatives make sense. We would have a generation of new economic activity which would result in additional jobs, lower UIC pay-outs, lower welfare pay-outs, more jobs, therefore more sales taxes, personal taxes, and corporate taxes collected. That would be a way to bring in more revenue to reduce the deficit. Not only that, reducing interest rates by 2.5 per cent would save an incredibly large amount of accumulated debt. If 2.5 per cent was knocked off the cost of $320 billion, billions of dollars would be saved.
Why wouldn't someone with the brains of a Minister of Finance not do that? Why would he not do something that everyone is advocating? Every premier in the country has come to Ottawa on a number of occasions and said: "For goodness sakes, give our regions an opportunity and drop the interest rate down two or three percentage points". However, the Government refuses to do that. It refuses to take action that would result in economic activity, decreased unemployment levels, and
Excise Tax Act
increased opportunities for entrepreneurs, builders and workers. The Government has a better idea: add more taxes on the people who are presently working.
I believe that we are desperately close to a tax revolt. I am not sure what form that tax revolt may take, but on balance Canadians know that they pay too much and will not take it any more. When they get the next opportunity to evaluate the Government and say whether or not they support it continuing in office, there is no question in my mind that those people are going to state that, in spite of some of them being half-decent people, we cannot afford it any longer. They cannot afford to raise their families, continue in business, or continue in farming. People have been pressed too hard.
As parliamentarians, one of the concerns that we must have, and about which the Government ought to be worried, is the development of the underground economy as a result of people's loss of faith in our tax system. Now billions of dollars of transactions are taking place underneath the table. There are no records and no taxes being paid. The best estimate of the size of this sector of our economy is that between $60 billion and $120 billion of transactions every year are moving underground because people have lost faith in the system.
They know that while they work and struggle to pay taxes, many people do not pay any taxes. Perhaps some people who live down the block do not pay any income taxes at all, be they individuals or high-income earners. You and I both know, Mr. Speaker, there are many people earning $200,000 or $500,000 a year who do not pay any income tax and are able to use the various loopholes. The person who is struggling in a small business, the backbone of the country in terms of employment, knows that while he or she is paying a lot of income tax, Alcan Aluminum does not pay anything, not a single cent. Hees International does not pay anything. Some years the Bank of Montreal does not pay anything. The Royal Bank of Canada does not pay anything.
Why do we not change the system? I wonder if one of the reasons, and I hate to say it but it is a suspicion of mine when one sees which large profitable corporations that do not pay any income tax give financial support to in terms of political Parties, lo and behold, the Conservatives get the lion's share, the Liberals get a fair share, in

June 6, 1989
Excise Tax Act
case they form a Government again, and the one Party that does not get any hand-outs from the Bank of Montreal or the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce or the Royal Bank is the New Democratic Party. We do not take that type of money. Why does this improper, unjust, biased system remain? I suspect that might play some role in why some of the legislation does not change to resolve it.
I think it is now time to be specific. We are discussing the principle of the Bill, and I want to mention some items. We have to warn Canadians about what this Government is going to do to them. A lot of damage has already been done, but the big blow is yet to come. Talking about the damage so far, the Government wants to increase the sales tax on construction material at a time when our economy is very sensitive in terms of its recovery, particularly in the regions of Canada where the construction industry drives a lot of the employment opportunities. If there is a lot of housing, office and plant construction, not only are there jobs in building, but all of the infrastructure that goes into those buildings, all of the manufacturing, all of the service industries and so on. The Government says, we think we have got a good idea. We are going to increase the sales tax on construction material. Why would a Government that has any brains want to increase the cost of building houses, factories and office complexes? That is what the Government is doing, and it just perplexes me.
The Government is going to slap the usual sales tax increases on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products. These are up from 18 per cent to 19 per cent. That is an area that is going to get hit, I suppose, on a regular basis. Again it just drives up the cost of living for so many people.
It is going to increase the sales tax on telecommunications and programming services from 10 per cent to 11 per cent beginning June 1. That sales tax on telecommunications has already been introduced. Then there will be an increase in the sales tax on all other goods to which it applies from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent. Where does this end, Mr. Speaker? There will be an increase in the excise tax on gasoline by one cent a litre beginning April 28, then again on January 1, 1990 as well as a
further 1 per cent per litre increase on leaded gasoline beginning April 28, 1989.
It does not sound like much when you look at it on an individual basis: one cent per litre on gasoline, a few cents on a carton of cigarettes, a 1 per cent increase in telecommunications costs, a 1 per cent increase on all construction materials. But when it is added up carefully, what it means to the average family-we have done some very thorough analysis and I am going to define the average family as being a family of four individuals with two working adults with two children and with a combined family income of $44,000. Some people will make more than that and some less, but that is your average combined income in Canada today from the cities of central Canada and into the regions. When you add it up, what does this one budget so far mean in terms of additional costs? It means an addition of $710 per family. We know how in 1984, 1985, 1986, 1987 the Conservatives increased all of those taxes year after year, budget after budget, but on top of all of that, this is an extra $710 per family.
What is silent, of course, is the national sales taxes coming next year. There is no mention in this particular Bill of that, but I think I would be remiss if I did not at least refer to it. It is stage two. This is the softening-up punch and the big one coming on January 1,1990 is going to knock them right out.
What is it going to cost? Leaving aside next year's budget that will probably end up being more, this average family with two people, two children and earning an income of $44,000, it is going to cost them next year an additional $1,000 a year in sales taxes. It will be applied to everything. If you get your hair cut, you are going to be paying an extra 9 per cent. When you go to the movies, you are going to be paying an extra 9 per cent. When you go bowling, you will be paying 9 per cent. When you fill out your will, you will be paying 9 per cent-9, 9, 9 everywhere you go. That is why we call this the beginning of the largest tax grab in Canadian history because next year it is going to be worse.
Your constituents, Mr. Speaker, are living in Edmonton and the Hon. Minister of State (Forestry) (Mr. Oberle) has a number of his constituents living in Prince George and Dawson Creek and a little further west. Both of you will know that an extra $1,000 per family in many cases cannot be handled. That is $700 this year, an extra $1,000 next year, $1,700 out of the pocket of every

family in Edmonton, Red Deer, Prince George, Kamloops, Montreal, Toronto. It is a form of highway robbery.
There is something sinister at work here, and I am not going to suggest that any Minister has had sinister motives by imposing this. I do think it is a plain ordinary tax grab, but what does it mean in the regions of Canada where for every family you pluck out $1,700 in sales and excise taxes and take it down to Ottawa to be used in some cases for rather questionable purposes? What it means is that $1,700 a family will not be in Prince George, $1,700 a family will not be in Edmonton. For all those families circulating between the businesses during the year it will be plucked out in sales taxes and excise taxes and sent down to Ottawa. It means that we are going to be curtailing business opportunities; in other words, the ability of local small businesses to do more business in the future. The money just will not be there. The disposable income just will not be there. When you reach in and pull $1,000 out of your pocket every single year from now on, on top of all the other money you pull out, you will not have that money to spend locally on a pair of new snow tires or some children's running shoes.
This national sales tax is actually going to put a tax on children's clothing, running shoes, lunch kits, books, and hats. When you think of it, it is rather a dastardly kind of tax. Yet, while this is taking place, there is no minimum corporate tax being introduced. There is no effort to reduce interest rates. There is no interest reducing the huge corporate loopholes that exist.
I want to refer to some of those corporate loopholes. When one looks at the corporate loopholes and one adds up what they cost taxpayers in taxes not collected, it comes to almost $30 billion. In other words, corporations, if they were paying taxes as most people do, would be paying an extra $30 billion. What is our deficit a year? It is about $30 billion. So the deficit we have is the money that we essentially lose in terms of corporate loopholes. I would ask anyone to find anywhere in our country a single tax lawyer, tax expert or accountant to identify a single corporate loophole where we get good return on the money that we lose.
Excise Tax Act
I have asked some of my colleagues to use this debate to identify which corporate loopholes give us value for money. The financial advisers, tax lawyers and accountants that I have heard from cannot identify one, at least not in public. They like them because corporations get good deals. I challenge anyone here or anyone listening or watching to identify a single corporate tax exemption that costs taxpayers money and lost revenue where we get more than that investment in the long term. I do not think it can be done.
I ask the question: when you add up the $30 billion in lost taxes, is it worth it? What are we getting for it? This is an analysis that must be done. If we are going to slap every working family with an extra $1,700 in sales and excise taxes, surely to goodness at the same time we should be spending time looking at other ways and means of increasing income as opposed to simply relying on those same taxpayers that have none of these tax incentive programs of which to take advantage. The few that they did have have now been eliminated, such as the regular tax deductions for medicare, medical costs and so on as well as the investment income. Now they have to be declared as well. Where are we going?

speechtext:
My hon. friend, the Minister of State for Forests, indicates that he is going to Kamloops on Thursday. When he has the opportunity to talk in Kamloops, I hope he will explain the value of the national sales tax that takes effect next year.
There is another problem associated with this national sales tax of which the Minister will be aware. A 9 per cent increase on all goods and services will obviously increase the cost of living. The cost of a haircut will go up 9 per cent. The price of children's shorts will go up 9 per cent. The cost of running shoes will go up 9 per cent. The cost of everything will increase by 9 per cent.
What will the Governor of the Bank of Canada do in his usual knee-jerk reaction when he sees the cost of living go up by 9 per cent? He will predict that inflation will rise by some 3 per cent, making the inflation rate in Canada about 7 per cent or 8 per cent. John Crow, the

June 6, 1989
Excise Tax Act
Governor of the Bank of Canada, will flip out and say that now is the time to increase interest rates substantially-
Not only is the Government going to hit consumers with $710 worth of sales and excise taxes, and on New Year's Day hit them with another 9 per cent sales tax across the board for another $1,000 out of the pockets of every family in Canada, the Governor of the Bank of Canada will surprise Canadians by jacking up interest rates immediately to curtail any increase in inflation.
Canadians cannot and will not take it any more. There is a limit. Canadians will no longer stand for it because of the discrimination in our tax system. They know that while Bill C-20 will result in many additional taxes for them other people will pay nothing.
I hope my hon. friends across the way will stand in their places during this debate and explain why they think this is a good idea. I hope they can explain how ordinary families can be taxed, while companies like Hees International, Cadillac Fairview, Alcan Aluminium, and Brascan do not pay any taxes in many years.
I ask my hon. friends opposite to explain the benefits of this policy and to explain why they believe an increase in these taxes at this time is a good idea when the Government at the same time is dismantling the Canadian economy as part of the trade deal.
The construction aspect of these tax increases is particularly interesting. I had an opportunity to speak to the Interior Construction Association in British Columbia about what it thought of this recent government initiative. I asked whether it thought an increase in the tax on construction materials made much sense.
I was rather astounded by the association's response that it had been to Ottawa to talk to some of the cabinet Ministers about this construction tax and thought it was told that the Government would actually eliminate the tax on construction materials. It is not surprising that it was before November 21 that the Government informed the association that it would actually eliminate tax on construction material.
The elimination of such a tax would make much sense in terms of kick starting the construction industry into high gear, to say nothing of what it would do for the forest industry in light of the additional home construction across the country. That too would have incredible spin-off for job creation, investment, and economic development.
Not only did the Government not eliminate the tax on construction material, it decided to increase it, to the disbelief of the construction industry.
I will not say that the industry was misled or misinformed, because that would be too obvious. However, it is perplexed at how the Government thinks this will help the economy or generate additional economic activity and revenue to the Treasury.
Perhaps I have said enough for the moment on this matter of taxes. The Bill we are debating represents an unprecedented tax grab. This debate will be the acid test to see whom Members represent in the House. While I do not know about members of the Liberal Party I assume they will oppose this measure.

I have not heard members on the government side say that they will represent their constituents this time as opposed to supporting a Minister of Finance who should not be there. Every financial writer in the country I know has said he should not be the Minister of Finance, but the Minister does not listen and simply stumbles ahead.
This is a test to see whether Conservative Members opposite represent the construction industry in their constituencies. If they do, they will surely not suggest that an increase in tax on construction materials will be appropriate.
Will they represent ordinary working families? If so, I do not think ordinary working families want to see an increase of $1,700 a year on an already incredibly high tax burden that is weighing them down. Do Hon. Members want an inflationary factor introduced with the introduction of a new sales tax? If they really want to hold down inflation in an effort to keep interest rates down, they will vote against this Bill.
Let me return to the whole matter of the legitimacy of this initiative in the first place. The Minister of Finance said that the federal sales tax he would introduce will be revenue neutral. Subsequently he said that it would really generate a whooping $23.5 billion a year in revenue.

This will be a massive tax grab by an illegitimate Minister in a Budget that should not proceed, through legislation that we should not be debating.
How does this affect our international reputation? What do countries throughout the world think about Canada when they see its Government loading such an incredible debt on working Canadians, a small portion of the population, while letting others go tax exempt? What does it say about a Minister of Finance and a Government that will do nothing about these leaks of budget information to privileged people in advance?
The best barometer to judge this is the money markets. There was a downward movement of the Canadian dollar as a reflection of the loss of faith in the Minister. I assume they are waiting for him to resign. They will be waiting for that good news for a long time.
We oppose Bill C-20, even its title. Normally, the Opposition opposes various clauses of a Bill. However, when we are eventually asked if we support the title of this Bill, we will have to say no because it is not accurate. The title should read: "A massive Canadian Government tax grab of working families". We hope that government Members will speak for their constituents, do the honourable thing and vote against this Bill so we will not have to examine it clause by clause in committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND THE EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-20, a Bill that will increase certain taxes. When we look at tax increases, we wonder, and I am sure Canadians are wondering, why we have these tax increases. Why did the Government take a step that is not necessarily very popular? I don't think many Canadians are delighted to hear they will have to pay more taxes. So why? Because, Mr. Speaker, and we often forget this, because the figures involved are enormous!
We must remember that in 1984, when this Government was elected, the national debt, in other words, the money Canada owed, was $200 billion. In other words, before 1984, over the years from, let us say, 1968 to 1984, the Government of the time annually spent more money than it was receiving in the Treasury, and it did that for 20 years, leaving the Conservative Government which took its place a bill for $200 billion. I often hear Opposition Members say: Yes, but you made it even worse. I agree, Mr. Speaker, that the national debt has increased by $120 billion since 1984, but if we calculate the interest charges paid annually since 1984 on their debt, these charges add up to $120 billion. So since 1984, if we exclude the interest charges on the debt that was a legacy from the previous Government, this government has had a balanced budget practically every year. However, we now have a situation where our debt is $320 billion.
Expressed in figures more readily understood by you and me, this means 3 million per hour. Our national debt, the money Canada owes, is increasing by $3 million per hour or $80 million every day, just because a previous Government spent a lot more money than it was able to collect. So now, Mr. Speaker, we have a situation where some very vigorous concrete measures must be taken if we are to control our annual deficit and the national debt, which has grown to enormous proportions.
Last week I was talking to people in the riding of Trois-Rivieres, as the Hon. Member for the NDP said, to small business people, Mr. Speaker, people who have a business and employees, and so forth, who are aware of the national debt problem, and who are in favour of the measures that have been taken, although they realize they will have to pay a little more.
The Canadian people, Mr. Speaker, want a Government whose first goal is a healthy economy, because a healthy economy means new jobs, and new jobs in turn mean bread and butter for everybody. And if we are to have a healthy economy and new jobs, the starting point is good management putting our own house in order. This is what the last Budget is all about. This is what has been done with increases in certain taxes-19 per cent on liquor. I am not aware of anyone opposing increased taxes on liquor and tobacco products. Nine per cent on building materials is still less than the general federal

June 6, 1989
Excise Tax Act
sales tax. Starting January 1st, 1990, there will be an 11 per cent tax on communication services. Finally, the rate will be 13.5 per cent on every other product already subject to the federal sales tax!
It is interesting to note the Liberal Finance critic stated the federal sales tax was regressive. The federal sales tax as we know it is 65 this year. And I believe, Mr. Speaker, the time definitely has come to retire it. This is why we came up with a new tax, a new way of taxing, that will be introduced on January 1, 1991. But in the meantime we had to increase the existing tax. But the reason why this sales tax is not regressive is that we are the first Government to innovate, as you will recall, before 1984 the previous Liberal Government used to increase the federal sales tax, period! We have introduced and this is why I refer to our being innovative a refundable federal income tax credit on sales tax. In the case of adults in 1989 it increases from $70 to $100, and for children, from $35 to $50. In 1990, the credit for adults increases from $100 to $140, and for children, from $50 to $70. This means that in 1990, a family with two adults and two children with an income of $18,000 or less will receive $420 to make up for the increase in the federal sales tax.
When I hear a self-appointed finance expert suggest that tax is regressive, Mr. Speaker, I believe he is on the wrong track. Statistics reveal that with an amount of $420 the two-adult family with two children will not be affected at all by this tax increase. I referred to the $18,000 threshold, Mr. Speaker, because you know that this year it is set at $16,000. It will rise to $18,000 next year.
I heard the Hon. Member say that the federal sales tax costs more in remote regions such as that of my colleague from Newfoundland and others. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is precisely one of the reasons why our system has to be overhauled. The tax now applies at the manufacturer level. Nobody knows about it, it is hidden. Just ask your constituents who knows there is a 12 or 13.5 per cent manufacturer tax on practically all consumer goods.
In addition a number of provinces levy a sales tax on top of the federal sales tax. In other words the Canadian consumer, say in Quebec, now pays close to 23 or 24 per
cent in provincial and federal sales taxes. That is sheer lunacy! What we want is to levy a 9 per cent retailer sales tax on goods, products and services. This way the Canadian consumer will see for himself how much the tax costs because it will no longer be hidden. Since the tax will apply to all goods and services it will be the same everywhere, easy to collect and more equitable as well.
I repeat that we will not hit low income families because the refundable tax credit we have devised will be maintained and even paid in advance. To put it another way, when the new tax becomes effective on January 1, 1991 families will already have received their first advance cheques. That, Mr. Speaker, is what I call fairness, justice and innovation, something both Opposition Parties have not even thought of!
Mr. Speaker, in speeches on the Budget after it is presented or on any bill having to do with taxation, unfortunately, we never hear positive suggestions from the Liberals or New Democrats. What did they suggest to improve the tax system, as we are prepared to do, to lower the deficit while at the same time ensuring that the Canadian economy will continue to operate well as it has done? You know that nearly one and a half million jobs were created in the past four years. But why were the jobs created? They were created because there was a government that managed the economy in such a way that jobs were created.
Mr. Speaker, eleven years ago, in 1978, I was studying for my master's in taxation at the University of Sherbrooke and the professor, a brilliant tax expert, especially on the federal sales tax, Normand Guerin by name, said in 1978: "The present federal sales tax system is archaic and no longer meets the needs of the country, much less of manufacturers, business people and the general public".
He said: It is unfortunate that the government in power is afraid to make changes because it is very complicated and it is not necessarily easy to tell people, "There is a hidden 12 per cent tax. We mil abolish it and replace it with a 9 per cent tax that you will see". Certainly, the people must understand that there is now a 12 per cent tax, which will be replaced by a 9 per cent tax!

So, that Liberal Government never had the decency, the courage or the nerve to implement a system that would benefit everyone and that at the same time would help reach this Government's first objective: restoring public finances.
Mr. Speaker, I am flabbergasted when I realize that the Government of Canada will have to pay this year $39 billion only to cover the interest on the debt which the previous Liberal Government left us as a legacy. Imagine, $39 billion!
Mr. Speaker, you know as I do what we could do with so much money. If we did not have to pay our national debt, we would have money a-plenty for Old Age Security pensions, daycare programs, research and development, environmental protection, etc. But we are saddled with this burden, we have this almost grotesque problem to solve before even considering any further investments in social, economic and cultural programs.
I was listening a while ago to a Member of the New Democratic Party who claimed that many corporations do not pay any corporate income tax. I do not know just how many do not, but my Honourable friend failed as usual to indicate that the corporations who do not pay any income tax may have one of two perfectly legitimate reasons for not doing so.
One of these reasons could be that they might have incurred losses in previous years and had elected, pursuant to the Income Tax legislation, to apply these losses against their profits for the current year. But this is something which is available not only to corporations, but to ordinary Canadian men and women, including you, Mr. Speaker, as well as all the Members of this House. If your corporation came out the loser following a bad transaction in 1989, and if it shows a profit in 1990, you may apply this loss incurred in 1989 against your profit in 1990. You would certainly run the risk of being revilled by my NDP friend as one who does not pay income tax. I am not saying that he tried to mislead the public, but he certainly failed to thoroughly explain the fine points of the Income Tkx legislation as it applies to corporations and individuals.
Another reason which might explain why your corporation does not pay any income tax is if you have made a major investment which entitles you to amortization. It is a well-known fact that amortization is deemed an
Excise Tax Act
admissible expense which can be applied against a corporation's profit.
These are the two reasons which might explain why you are not paying any income tax.
The Hon. Member forgot to mention on the other hand that it was this Conservative Government which has implemented since 1986 a minimum income tax scheme, so that individuals earning $100,000, $50,000 or $25,000 have a minimum income tax to pay. This obviously was an oversight on his part.
He also emphasized the fact that all Canadians will be paying more income tax. But he forgot to point out, Mr. Speaker, that with the 1988 tax reform 85 per cent of Canadians pay less income tax than before. That he forgot to mention. Eighty five per cent of Canadians pay less income tax and if I remember correctly, Mr. Speaker, one million Canadians do not pay income tax any more because of tax reform. Measures have been implemented and Canadians have realized it after filing their income tax returns this year.
Many residents of my constituency of Trois-Rivieres, who were skeptical after tax reform was announced, have told me: "Sir, you were right. It's true! We are paying less income tax for 1988 than 1987. Your reform is good and worthwhile." At the same time, companies and businesses have seen their income tax rates go up.
I think it is normal that businesses pay their fair share but we should bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that they are the ones that create the jobs in this country. If we had the same rationale as NDP Members, we would tax businesses 100 per cent. They would not make any profits at all and would only pay taxes.

speechtext: They would not be in business for long.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND THE EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
My colleague, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for the beautiful riding of Manicouagan (Mr. Langlois) made a quite logical and realistic comment: "They would not be in business for long". As a matter of fact, if we want our Canadian businesses to make progress, they should make normal profits, they should pay a reasonable tax rate to be able to reinvest then-profits, thus make a move forward and automatically create new jobs in the process.

June 6, 1989
Mr. Speaker, if we compare the 1980-84 Liberal Government with ours regarding job creation, we created 10 times more jobs than the previous Liberal Government. Even better, 9 jobs out of 10 that we created were permanent, while under the Liberal Government, 9 jobs out of 10 were temporary. You will recall, M. Speaker, the nice programs implemented by the Liberals about painting fences, doing housework, repairing different residences, presbyteries, etc. They were calling that job creation. Certainly, the community that was offered a grant was very proud and happy. But those were not permanent jobs. When the construction is over and the painting done, the job is gone!
So there was a "work/no work" cycle. That was the cycle we had from 1980 to 1984, but now, we see the real job creation that has taken place, despite tax increases, Mr. Speaker, since 1984.
No company or government can go into debt all the time and hope that one day the debt problem will solve itself. Once again, Mr. Speaker, I challenge the Members of the other two parties to come up with ideas-concrete, realistic suggestions-for, first, reducing the deficit and, second, creating jobs, while solving the national debt problem.
Mr. Speaker, you are indicating to me that my time has expired. Thank you. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I urge all Hon. Members of the House to vote for the adoption of Bill C-20 as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, while anxious to reduce the deficit, the federal Government proposes to finance a very costly project named OSLO for the extraction of oil from tar sands. This would significantly increase carbon dioxide pollution at a time
when scientists are urging a reduction if we really want to slow down the global warming trend.
If the Government is really concerned about global warming, if the Government cares about the greenhouse effect it must put a stop to the OSLO oil sands project and any other fossil fuel megaproject which increases our dependence on oil.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Epp) is a minister of the environment. His energy policies are of great environmental importance. Oil extraction megaprojects and nuclear power are not the foundations on which to build a sound environmental energy policy. If the Minister of Energy is to keep the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on sustainable development, he should cancel these projects.

Mr. Speaker, the Solidarity Union movement, outlawed until two months ago, appears headed for a massive victory in Sunday's Polish elections.
Millions of Poles eagerly and gladly seized their first opportunity since World War II to exercise their limited yet very significant freedom through secret ballots to vote against the Communist Government and for their Solidarity candidates.
I am sure that all Members of this House would want to join with me in congratulating the Solidarity movement, and its leaders for their persistence and courage over the years and for their excellent performance Sunday, June 4, in this historic milestone in democratic reform in Poland. Father Popieluszko would have been overjoyed to have seen what took place in Poland on Sunday.
I urge the Government of Canada to do all in its power to support the democratic reform process under way in Poland today.
June 6, 1989

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, much of the world is looking and remembering D-Day. We Canadians in particular have a special reason to recall June 6, 1944.
This morning representatives of all Canadian units involved in D-Day and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Merrithew) were at the Beny-Sur-Mer Canadian war cemetery in Normandy. There are over 2,000 Canadians buried there, young men killed either on D-Day itself or in the follow-up drive to push inland.
We naturally think of D-Day as an event colossal in scope but in truth D-Day was like any other battle. Success or failure depended on a series of individual engagements.
Today let us bless the memory of those Canadians who fought those individual battles. Some are buried in Beny-Sur-Mer. Some went on to liberate The Netherlands less than a year later. All helped to restore freedom to Europe. Our gratitude has not faded with time, and let us hope it never will.
Hear, hear!

maintopic: CANADIAN CENTRE FOR OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY
CANADIAN CENTRE FOR OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 19, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. James) handed a little note to the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, the contents of which will spell death to the centre and its work by 1991. Their demand for full cost recovery by the centre is nothing less than unjustifiable discrimination. Why the double standard?
If 1,000 Canadians per year were to die, 20,000 permanently disabled and hundreds of thousands suffer illness or injury due to any one choice of personal life style, unhealthy diet, or smoking or drinking, the Government would and does pay the bill, however inadequately, for research and dissemination of free public health information and warnings.
But if you are a Canadian worker who will, in fact, suffer these casualty rates every year as a result of simply working for a living-not much choice there-the Conservatives say "Root, hog or die" and pay your own way.
This is not a class act. This is an act of class discrimination. I urge the Government to reverse its decision, restore funding to the centre and allow Canadian workers equal access to the information which will grant them the right to work and to live in the safest environment possible.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in the House to bring to the attention of the Government a matter of grave concern.
A publication of the Library of Parliament Research Branch entitled "Railway Safety, 1988" points out that more people are killed at level crossings than in derailments and collisions. The Foisey Report and the inquiry into the Mississauga derailment addressed the latter two issues. These inquiries also point out safety concerns regarding crews and equipment. A constituent believes that an inquiry into level crossing accidents would point out several deficiencies with inadequate visibility being the most common.
On November 12, 1988, three young people were killed and in 1975 two people were killed at Mile 46.76 of the CPR mainline north of Cambridge. In correspondence and interviews with my constituents there is reason to believe that these accidents could have been avoided if proper warning signals were in place. As five people have now died at this crossing, I urge the Department of Transport to install automatic railway crossing signals at side road 30 in the Township of Puslinch.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow, June 7, Sikh Canadians will join the 15 million Sikh adherents world-wide to commemorate the execution of a great religious leader, the Guru Arjan Devji, who compiled the Sikh teachings into a single volume
