5. Q 31
that became the scriptural base of Sikhism. The Guru Arjan Devji was executed for his refusal to renounce the principles of his faith.
More than 100,000 Canadians adhere to Sikhism. Their teachings have since the 16th century stressed the equality of men and women, opposed discrimination in all its forms and emphasized philanthropy, family and the maintenance of a moral, responsible and selfless everyday life.
Sikh Canadians have made, and continue to make, a great contribution to Canada. They hold firmly the noble principles of their faith and their origin. I would like to convey to them my respect and admiration and to join with them in commemoration of this special day of remembrance.

subtopic: COMMEMORATION OF EXECUTION OF GURU ARJAN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of National Access Awareness Week, I think it would be appropriate to ask ourselves individually and collectively whether we are really doing enough to help disabled people participate fully in community life. The disabled have the same basic needs as the rest of the population. However, obstacles have sometimes hindered their autonomy-in transportation, housing, employment, recreation or education.
To pay tribute to the communities that have done the most to integrate the disabled in each of the five areas that I just named, the Department of the Secretary of State together with the Federation of Canadian Municipalities is sponsoring the Five-Star Community Prize Program. The Five-Star Community Prize is the highest award a community can obtain in recognition of its efforts to integrate the disabled. Mr. Speaker, many organizations in my riding are working on this and I am sure that they all deserve this prize!

Mr. Speaker, later this month at the beginning of the tourist season on Prince Edward Island, Air Canada will end its direct flights from Ottawa to Charlottetown. This move will add time and money to the cost of doing business on the Island. It will discourage tourists from visiting and it will create an inconvenience for Islanders. It is also insulting that a provincial capital is losing its direct flight from the nation's capital for economic reasons.
Economics is all this Government seems to care about. But 125 years ago when the Fathers of Confederation met in Charlottetown to plan this country, they had a vision for Canada which included more than economics. So I urge this Government to reconsider its transportation policy because the people of Prince Edward Island deserve better.

Mr. Speaker, during the past few months there has been some considerable discussion as to which area of Canada truly deserves the title of "Lobster Capital of Canada".
Some have suggested Shediac, New Brunswick because of its long history of participation in this industry. But clearly that participation is dwindling. Some have suggested Yarmouth, Nova Scotia because so many lobsters have been shipped through that historic port.
But surely so distinguished a title can only rightfully be attributed to the place in Canada where the most lobsters are caught, the most lobsters are landed, where the dollar value of landings is the greatest, and that place clear and away is Shelburne County, Nova Scotia.
Hear, hear!

Accordingly, with the mandate given to me by the people of South Shore, Nova Scotia, I hereby declare and proclaim, without fear of retribution or

contradiction, that Shelburne County, Nova Scotia is the lobster capital of Canada.
Furthermore, I would like to bring to the attention of Parliament and all Canadians and issue an invitation to all to attend the Third Annual Shelburne County Lobster Festival to be held this weekend, June 9 to June 12 in the Lobster Capital of Canada, Shelburne County, Nova Scotia.
EXPIRY OF FEDERAI^PROVINCIAL AGREEMENTS

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, forest resource development agreements between the federal Government and six provinces expired on March 31. Yesterday, at the signing of the Constitution of the Canadian Woodlot Owners Federation, the president of the organization said that the lack of new agreements is wreaking havoc on planning by woodlot owners and other producers in the forest sector. He went on to say that further delays will be disastrous.
Recent Budget cuts clearly indicate that this Government is prepared to sacrifice the future of the forest industry. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will be in B.C. this week to address a Conservative Party fund-raising dinner. In light of the Minister of Forests failure to deliver forestry agreements, the Prime Minister should make a commitment to British Columbia and this country to fund forest agreements.

Mr. Speaker, the situation is desperate at the Port of Churchill in northern Manitoba.
After signing a $90 million agreement just four years ago to rebuild the port, the present Conservative Government has allowed the Canadian Wheat Board and CN to renege on their commitments. Just two weeks ago, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) confirmed that no grain shipments will be made through the port this year. Rather than look for alternate and creative ways of
utilizing the port, the Government has preferred to ignore the problem.
I would like to draw the attention of the House to an innovative proposal which has been put forward by the Member from Niakwa in the Manitoba legislature. He has introduced a private members' resolution recommending that the federal Government designate Churchill as the port for federal commodity and foreign aid purposes. Rather than losing Churchill to further neglect, the federal Government could give this new mandate to ship all foreign food in through the port of Churchill and thereby provide aid for the countries of Africa, and to provide major stimulus and economic health for a port in our own country.
I applaud and support this creative initiative. I recommend it to the federal Government as a way of dealing with an important port in an important province.

Mr. Speaker, last weekend I worked with a number of citizens in communities in my riding, Bolton and Burlington, doing something for the environment.
We did not have a meeting. We did not talk. We did not prepare a report or pass any resolution. Instead, we got our hands and our boots dirty, scouring ditches for litter and pulling old car parts from a creek.
There were not as many people out helping as I had hoped, but I think this tells us something valuable. This is Environment Week. It comes at a time when our public opinion polls show that environmental concerns are of the utmost importance to average Canadians. It is still easier to talk about the environment than to do something about it. My weekend experiences certainly reinforced that.
It is time for a change in attitudes. It is time to recognize that we all have an activist role to play when it comes to ensuring that future generations of Canadians have a clean world to inherit from us.
In our everyday lives, we have choices about buying groceries with excessive packaging, about the disposal of paint cans and batteries, about whether we substitute natural substances for harmful household cleaners, and about conserving our water and making sure we drive in a way that does not create air pollution. Protecting the

June 6, 1989
environment is not somebody else's job, Mr. Speaker. It is yours and mine, so it is time we all did something about it.

Mr. Speaker, over
800,000	work days are lost annually by Canadians to disabling injuries and over 440 lives are lost annually in Canada due to industrial accidents.
As a result, more than $7 billion is spent annually to cover medical expenses, compensation for lost earnings, pensions, insurance and loss of production. Accidents carry a high price. Recently, the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System was imposed by Governments across Canada. It ensures access to data and instruction on how to handle dangerous material by workers. This, however, did little to change the working environment.
Canadian occupational health and safety statistics are abysmal and becoming worse. In spite of this, the Government has seen fit to decrease funding by over 11 per cent towards occupational health and safety.
Canadian workers do not deserve more cuts, Mr. Speaker. They deserve action and more direct input into resolving and eliminating occupational hazards in the workplace.

subtopic: FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF STORMING OF GOLDEN TEMPLE
FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF STORMING OF GOLDEN TEMPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today marks the fifth anniversary of the storming of the Golden Temple in the Punjab by the Indian army. It is therefore appropriate to reflect on the ongoing problems faced by the Sikh community in India.
Amnesty International reports allegations that dozens of political prisoners in Indian prisons have died after being tortured while in police custody and also that there have been staged encounters by the police in which political activists were killed. Other reports indicate that
hundreds of Sikhs are being kept in jail awaiting trial, many without any formal charges against them.
Included among those imprisoned is a Canadian landed immigrant, Mr. Amaijit Singh Sohi, a member of the Punjabi Literary Association of Edmonton. He went to India last April to work in drama and human rights groups, and was arrested in November while attending a convention. He was charged with being a Sikh terrorist. There is apparently no evidence to support the charge, but Mr. Sohi remains in detention.
Mr. Speaker, the vast majority of Sikh people favour a peaceful resolution of the difficulties in the Punjab. Continued harassment and repression by Indian authorities contribute nothing to such a resolution. I urge the Canadian Government to use its influence and express our concern to India regarding that country's treatment of Sikhs, and particularly Canadian Sikhs who visit India.

Mr. Speaker, in the context of National Environment Week in Canada, I wish to remind Canadians that there are two distinct perspectives evolving in the world's approach to managing our planet earth, both for our and future generations.
Dr. Jim MacNeill, Secretary of the World Commission on Environment and Development, has made these two perspectives very clear. The first is environmental protection, the area with which we have thus far been primarily concerned. It is critical that we intensify our efforts to clean and protect our environment from the ways we abuse and misuse its resources. We should understand though that in so doing, we are generally reacting to effects from our activities.
The second is sustainable development, the more recent recognition that merely reacting to protect our environment is not enough. We must do more. We must pro-act to manage our future use of the world's resources so that we may cause both those resources and humanity to be sustained in perpetuity.
In both of these perspectives-environmental protection and sustainable development-the world has much to accomplish. Canada can set that lead.
June 6, 1989

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Thrner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question or two for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Canadians and the world watch in horror as events unfold of the terrifying spectacle in the most populous nation on earth. The world watches as young Chinese are killed because Government leaders there are playing power games and because the Chinese authorities refuse to recognize the legitimacy of a valued and brave struggle for freedom.
When does he anticipate that Canadians will have been evacuated from China? How many Canadians does the Government expect will remain in that country?
I would like to ask him whether, upon reflection overnight, he has come to a decision, which I urge him to take, to use our seat on the Security Council of the United Nations to initiate a motion of censure in that body against the People's Republic of China.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition for his questions. He placed three.
A chartered Canadian Airlines International aircraft is on its way to Beijing. It will be leaving Beijing, carrying more than 200 Canadians out. It will be leaving in about 12 hours from now en route to Tokyo. There are about 210 Canadians who have indicated an interest in being on the aircraft. There are still spaces available.
It is our intention to remove all Canadians from Beijing with the exception of about 20 of the more senior officials of the Department of External Affairs who will remain on site for the foreseeable future. If circumstances require their removal, then that will be done.
At the moment we are not recommending the evacuation from other points in China of other Canadians who are there. There are about 300 other Canadians else
Oral Questions
where in China. We have identified the whereabouts of virtually all of them, although we are checking to make sure that we know the exact location of tourists or business persons who might be in some more remote parts of the country. We have arrangements in place, if necessary, to bring them out.
We have dispatched today a Canadian Air Force plane which will stand by on a military base in Japan in case there is a need for further evacuation.
With respect to the actions in the United Nations, as the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and other Members of the House made clear last night, this country has been very active in the recent and, until this point, progressive history of China. We have excellent credentials to exercise a leadership role in responding to these tragic events.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition will know the judgment of the Secretary General of the United Nations who drew attention yesterday to the requirements of the Charter of the United Nations, that the United Nations should abstain from intervention in regard to matters that are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of states. Obviously, disorder and conflict in a country as large and as powerful as China cannot long remain an internal matter.
One hour ago I was in touch with Ambassador Fortier in the United Nations. He is continuing his active consultations with members of the Security Council and other members of the United Nations to explore every possible and practical opportunity for Canada to exercise leadership in allowing the United Nations also to express its outrage at these actions and perhaps to have an influence that could encourage Chinese leaders to adopt a more positive, less dangerous course.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the thoroughness of the Minister's answers on the information I requested in the first part of my question.
I would urge him with respect to the United Nations to recognize that human rights know no boundaries or frontiers and that this is an issue involving human kind. I know he wants to act prudently. I hope that he acts

June 6, 1989
Oral Questions
decisively on behalf of the people of Canada in the United Nations.
Could the Secretary of State be good enough to advise us what consultations his Government has had with the United States, Great Britain, and other nations as to the possible consequences for the world if the current thrust of the Chinese Government persists in that country?
Will the Chinese Government be advised that we in this country will have great difficulty in accepting a transfer of Efong Kong to the jurisdiction of the People's Republic of China if these events continue?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition and the House would expect, we are in active consultation with a range of other countries, not simply our normal allies but a range of other countries with an interest in the stability of China. We are doing that bilaterally. We are doing it at the United Nations, particularly with regard to other members of the Security Council. To a limited degree we are exchanging information on the ground in Beijing among missions that are there.
There are a number of other questions that will have to be faced in the days, perhaps early days to come with relation, for example, to the status of the Chinese application to the GATT, with relation to the future of CIDA projects, with relation to the EDC line of credit, and with relation to the specific question the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has raised concerning the status of Hong Kong.
We are fortunate in this country to have very experienced officials who have spent a lot of time in China. We are making full use of their expertise.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition would agree that we do not want to make any of those decisions too quickly, but we want to be in a position to take them immediately when the time is appropriate. I hope that we
are following the course that I believe will put us in that position.

subtopic: REQUEST AS TO PLANNING OF HUMANITARIAN AID

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST AS TO PLANNING OF HUMANITARIAN AID
speechtext: Finally, Mr. Speaker, could the Minister inform the House of the new steps that have been taken or will be taken by Canada to provide humanitarian aid through the Red Cross or other volunteer organizations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST AS TO PLANNING OF HUMANITARIAN AID
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made it clear last night during the emergency debate here in the House that Canada is prepared to offer humanitarian aid, in response to official requests from the Red Cross and other organizations. So far, I don't think we have received any official requests, but I made it clear that Canada is prepared to make an affirmative response to such requests.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Immigration and it too concerns the situation in China.
Yesterday's announcement to halt deportations of all rejected Chinese refugees for 60 days, along with the Secretary of State's decision not to send back some 4,500 Chinese students presently studying in Canada, was an exemplary response to the tragedy we have all witnessed during the past few days. I commend the Minister and her colleagues in the Government for those decisions.
Hear, hear!

Last year, only 2,700 people were landed in Canada from the People's Republic of China. Today the Canadian-Chinese community, which numbers somewhere in the area of 400,000 across Canada, is somewhat concerned for the safety of family members, not only in Beijing but throughout China.
Given the circumstances of the events in China, and the low acceptance rate in the last number of years of Chinese citizens, is the Government prepared to specifically relax the family class and the assisted family class criteria in order that more Canadian-Chinese families will have an easier and more successful time in sponsoring relatives from China to Canada?

Mr. Speaker, none of the above. What was signed and agreed to in Brussels is an important step forward in terms of process. The Vice-President of the European Community, on behalf of the commission, agreed with Canada to establish a process that would be based upon two very important principles: one being the conservation of the stocks and the other being the principle of rational management.
The case that Canada has been making to the Europeans, to the Community; making bilaterally when the Prime Minister met with the Prime Minister of Spain and the Prime Minister of Portugal; and has been making generally is that if current European overfishing practices continue, there will be no fish left for Canadians, no fish left for Europeans. speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was legislation standing in my name. It is quite clear that when the Acting Speaker was in the chair yesterday that he was seeing the clock and felt it was well within the rules that the question be put.
There is another question that must be addressed, and it relates to something that has been ongoing for some time. It is one thing to make an argument the day after that the clock was not seen accurately. However, the Hon. Member who just spoke, was not in his seat. In fact, he was speaking to the Whip of the Liberal Party at that time. When he was speaking to the Whip of the Liberal Party at the Whip's desk, the Acting Speaker called whether there was any further debate, and the NDP had exhausted the number of speakers they had in the House at that time. So there was the time-honoured attempt by the NDP to put forward a specious point of order in order that they could get the time past five o'clock so that the Speaker could not put the question.
That is what happened yesterday, and I believe the Acting Speaker was well within the rules of the House.
Mr. Speaker, with all due respect to the Hon. Minister, I must disagree. We all recognize that this place operates on goodwill.
On rules, too.

As well as rules.
At about five o'clock, there were considerable negotiations taking place between the parties. The Whips, Deputy Whips and Deputy House Leaders were discussing the matter of achieving unanimity on a motion that could be put before the House in terms of the Adjournment Debate later in the evening.
Just prior to five o'clock, when the Hon. Member was in the lobby watching the clock so that he could come in to participate in the debate, he noticed that the clock said 5 p.m. When the clock says 5 p.m., very clearly that is when the adjournment occurs in terms of the debate.
As Hansard points out on page 2579, it is very clear that five o'clock had arrived. After five o'clock is when the Acting Speaker then asked, "Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?''
It is very clear by reading Hansard that that was after five. Naturally, no one from the government side or the opposition side would be rising to speak because five o'clock had come and passed.
What we are doing is suggesting that the vote scheduled to occur at six o'clock is out of order, that had the Speaker followed the traditional rules, followed the traditions of the House and been sensitive to the very important negotiations that were under way at that moment, no way would we have had the question put in a period after 5 p.m.
We are asking that you rule on this matter and suggest that we have two or three additional speakers, Members who were awaiting an opportunity to participate in this important debate. There was no filibuster effort, as the Minister knows. He rose. There were a few speakers and there is no suggestion of any effort to prolong the debate. He knows it is an important piece of legislation. There were two or three NDP Members interested in participating in the debate, but now they have been curtailed from participation at the second reading stage of this important legislation.
I assume it was an oversight on behalf of the Acting Speaker at the time. But, as Hansard points out very clearly, the question was put after five o'clock when we should have been on Private Members' Business.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, back in 1980, perhaps early 1981, I rose in the Chamber at some length on a question of privilege related to the clocks. It might be wise to check the precedents, but my recollection is that the Speaker at that time did indicate clearly to the Chamber that the clock in front of the Speaker was the dominant clock in terms of the Speaker's world. That was several years ago. I think that was part of what was said yesterday. I just draw your attention to the precedent.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if this House is going to be running on clocks that nobody sees except the Speaker, we have a problem. This House runs on good will, debate, and on the understanding that people can rise in their places and debate Bills on which they decide to speak. Liberals had no intention of speaking. It is true, since my name was
June 6, 1989

brought into the debate, that I was negotiating with the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) when the Speaker rose at five o'clock sharp and put the question. At that time, the Member ran to go to his seat because he wanted to object to that procedure and call for debate. That is what I was told, that is what I believe and, as far as I am concerned, the procedure yesterday was rather quick.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there is a way to resolve this situation. As my hon. friend, the Whip for the Official Opposition indicated, this House operates on rules, regulations, traditions and, most importantly, goodwill. There is no intention to cut off debate prematurely. The Official Opposition Whip has described accurately the effort of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) to get to his seat. It was simply a matter of wrong time viewed by the Acting Speaker. Perhaps there would be unanimous consent of the Members to not have the vote tonight and so allow those few Members an opportunity to complete their remarks at a later day.

Mr. Speaker, not to belabour the point but I am reminded by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Laporte), that when the Hon. Member for Kootenay West-Revelstoke (Mr. Kristiansen) started speaking, the clock in the Chamber showed 4.32 p.m. for a 20-minute speech followed by a 10-minute question and answer period. But the Member from Moose Jaw-Lake Centre was, in fact, on his feet at the time the Acting Speaker rose, trying to get the floor to pursue the remaining two minutes in terms of questions and answers. I think that should be taken into consideration and perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you might wish to check the very meticulous records kept at the table in front of you in terms of the start times for various speakers, because I know that that is what the Speaker has to adhere to.
In any case, I do want to remind you that the long-term result is to have one clock that we can all see so there can be no question about not seeing the clock unless we all agree that we are not going to see the clock.

Mr. Speaker, I would want to intervene briefly. I was present yesterday when the events took place as described by the Official Opposition Whip, and they were essentially as described. I would point out that if there is any question at all, it is whether or not there should be a deferred division. It is true that the Deputy House Leader for the New Democratic Party did try to make his way back to his seat to get the floor, but he had already spoken as had the other three Members of that Party who were present
Point of Order-Mr. Angus
in the House and there were only four Members in the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) who has been here for many years and who understands the working of this place as well as any of us has, of course, reduced the discussion to its essence.

Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
But that does not take away from the fact that there was a complaint here. Clearly, members of the New Democratic Party did not wish at that point to proceed in answer to the question put by the Acting Speaker. It was not-I have to very gently and with great courtesy correct the Hon. Minister-"Shall the debate continue?" or words to that effect. It was "Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?" Now, whether that was said before five o'clock or after five o'clock, we have to accept the word of the Acting Speaker who was in the chair at that time and has clearly indicated that he was watching the clock.
The point I want to make is this: There has been discussion about the fact that this place operates ultimately on goodwill and that is true. All I can say to my hon. friends in the New Democratic Party is that I accept that what happened was not what they intended to happen. I think that Hon. Members will agree with me. I have deliberately allowed some discussion on this so that the members of the NDP are entitled to make their point. I had the feeling that even in the strong representations they made they realize that the Speaker cannot go back to yesterday and undo what has been done. As the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier has pointed out, the House has taken a decision.
However, it is a caution to all of us, those in the chair and those on both sides of the Chamber, that we must be alert, we must be following debate carefully and we must do it in such a way that nobody feels at any time that he or she has been unfairly treated or in any way prejudiced in trying to present the point of view of a particular Member or the point of view of a particular Party.
I regret that there has been this dispute. But I think Hon. Members can understand that we must accept what the Acting Speaker says as to his own point of view with respect to time. We also have to accept and I have to so rule, according to what the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier has so clearly stated, which is absolutely correct procedurally, that I cannot go back and undo what happened yesterday even if some particular Members might feel aggrieved. All I can ask is the co-operation of the House to be sure that these things happen very seldom, if at all.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
that Bill C-21, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to open the debate on Bill C-21, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
As Members are aware, these changes are a part of the Government's Labour Force Development Strategy. As such, they should not be considered in isolation from other elements of the strategy designed to improve the amount and quality of training in the private sector.

In fact, Mr. Speaker, failure to come to terms with training concerns throughout our labour market will severely affect Canada's ability to compete in the future.
All Ministers in the Government have been looking at the issues we must address to make Canada more competitive, more confident, and more compassionate. This means asking some tough questions.
How can Canada compete when our private sector spends on training only half of what its U.S. competition spends? How can we give our workers the skills they need to provide them with a more secure personal future? How do we better help our less prosperous regions? Can we afford any longer to have the easiest entry into unemployment insurance of almost any western country? Is our unemployment insurance program doing all it can to help Canadians get back into the workforce quickly and permanently?
The answers which our Government has come up with are clear from the announcement that I made on April 11 and in Bill C-21 which I was proud to introduce on June 1.
June 6, 1989

We did not expect any or all of these initiatives to be popular with everyone. In many ways, they redefine roles and responsibilities and they challenge vested interests. But we know that our approach works and we have the record to prove it.
Since we came to office in 1984, our philosophy as a Government has recognized that the private sector is the key to the future success of the Canadian workforce and the Canadian economy. Privatization, deregulation, tax reform and free trade are all parts of the same agenda for revitalizing the Canadian economy to meet the requirements of increased globalization of markets and rapid technological change.

The Labour Force Development Strategy will build on the Canadian Jobs Strategy model by bringing the private sector-business and labour-together to set the course for each sector and industry.
In 1985, our Government radically changed the approach to employment programs. We ended the mishmash of more than 40 ineffective make-work programs with the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
We believe not in making work but in making jobs. Our new approach was to focus on the individual and his or her training needs. It also recognized that bureaucrats in Ottawa are not the people who should be determining what local labour market needs are. We brought in an approach that recognizes that the people who best know what is needed in a local economy are the people who live there.
Let us look at Bill C-21. Our Government believes that the unemployment insurance program can work better. The current variable entrance requirement was designed to reflect more closely the labour market differences across the country. However, with the many varying economic conditions across the country, the current system is too inflexible and limited. The result has been that people in areas such as Montreal, Moncton and St. John's face the same entrance requirements while facing very different employment prospects.

We have designed a new variable entrance requirement which is much more regionally sensitive. The result is that in areas of lower unemployment, where there are greater employment opportunities, Canadians have to wait a little longer to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. As well, if you live in a low unemployment region, the duration of the benefits will be
Unemployment Insurance Act
shorter. I stress that this will occur in areas where greater job opportunities exist.
As the unemployment rate rises, entrance requirements will be progressively easier to meet. Similarly, the duration of benefits available will reflect the varying degrees of difficulty that Canadians face in finding new jobs. The current entrance requirement ranges from 10 weeks to 14 weeks. We will increase the range from 10 weeks to 20 weeks, maintaining the 10-week requirement for regions with unemployment over 15 per cent.
The Government believes that the UI program must continue to reflect regional differences in unemployment. The new entrance requirements are therefore more regionally sensitive and fairer in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, those who are legitimately out of work, or who leave a job with good reason, deserve support. They will continue to receive it. The small minority who simply chooses not to work at various times should not be encouraged by a system paid for by all Canadians.

The UI system was not designed to serve that purpose. The Government has a responsibility to Canadians to see that the system helps those who genuinely need help and discourages those who just do not want to work.
Mr. Speaker, it is an irrefutable fact that in the world we now live in, people drive economic growth-"brainpower" and "skillpower"-and that our future growth will depend more than ever on a highly skilled, flexible labour force.
In individual terms, this means satisfaction and the rewards which go with better job qualifications.
Mr. Speaker, that is why under the Labour Force Development Strategy, the Government is doubling the money spent on training by the unemployment insurance program. There have been a lot of inaccurate statements made by Members opposite on what the Government is proposing in this area.

June 6, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
First, let me clearly state that the unemployment insurance program has been providing training to UI recipients for many years. This practice was initiated by the previous Liberal Government.

The UI account currently spends $255 million annually in income support for those who take training while on unemployment insurance. Many of these people need additional assistance. Through the Canadian Jobs Strategy, the Government also spends considerable funds to purchase the courses, to provide dependant care allowances and transportation costs for these UI recipients.
Mr. Speaker, under Bill C-21, clause 20, it will be possible to pay for a portion of the current CJS costs devoted to UI claimants out of the UI account. This makes room in the Canadian Jobs Strategy to pay for the programs outlined in the labour force development strategy which do not go directly to UI recipients.
We are doubling the funds allocated to section 26 training under this program. This is consistent with recommendation 40(a) of the report of the Standing Committee on Labour and Employment Immigration from the last Parliament on their study of the Forget Report to increase the use of section 26 training. Hon. Members can clearly see from Bill C-21 that UI funds will continue to be used to assist only UI recipients.
Another important aspect of this Bill is contained under clause 20. That is the provision for claimants to be able to receive assistance in helping them move to places where they may have found employment. Again, this is similar to the recommendation in the standing committee report that I mentioned earlier. I might add that this was a report signed by the employment critic for the Official Opposition, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand).
There were 90 recommendations.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
The funds freed up under the Canadian Jobs Strategy brought about by Clause 20 of Bill C-21 will allow redirecting $230 million under CJS to increased training activity in the private sector through co-operative programs. Our intent is to stimulate an additional $1.5 billion each year from the private sector for training from now until 1994.
We plan to spend $65 million annually on sectoral human resource planning. The pilot projects done to date have shown encouraging results. We will also be creating a new entry level skill program akin to the apprenticeship program which we believe will train an additional 40,000 to 50,000 people per year. We are quadrupling the funds that we provide for co-op education under CJS.
We will be doubling the budget of the Industrial Adjustment Service in response to its effectiveness in dealing with labour force adjustment.
In addition, under this section of the initiatives, we will be providing an additional $50 million to the Community Futures Program of the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
Finally, we will be providing an additional $50 million from CJS for training for social assistance recipients. Under this program, begun by our Government in 1986, the Government has committed $400 million to train
60,000	social assistance recipients annually. Together with provincial funds, this will bring total expenditures under this program to $800 million. It is a very successful program, Mr. Speaker.
It is in everyone's interest clearly that this approach work. Canadian productivity is lagging far behind most industrialized countries. As 60 per cent of the people who will be in the workforce in the year 2000 have already left school, the private sector will have to train and retrain those people if we are to remain competitive. That is why we believe that these expenditures will generate $1.5 billion in expenditures on training annually by the private sector, because we have seen this work before.
Someone mentioned older workers. Ours is a workforce increasingly dependent on Canadians who are 45 years of age and older. It is imperative that their talents and experience not be lost either through market changes or entrenched hiring practices. Our new strategy recognizes this phenomenon specifically by providing $100 million in new programming for older workers to complement existing programs. From an equity standpoint, the strategy recognizes that older workers do want to work and should have access to income protection past age 65. I should add that this means that older workers
June 6, 1989

will continue to pay premiums after age 65 if they choose to remain in the paid labour force.
Women have also changed the face and the faces of our labour force. We have recognized the importance of their participation and contribution by providing not only additional training, but also other supports through enhanced maternity, parental, and sickness benefits. Contrary to what some critics in the business community may say, these supports are essential to them as well to maintain a highly trained and effective Canadian workforce in the 1990s.
Women represent 52 per cent of our population, and that is 52 per cent of the talent in this country. They are a key to our competitiveness in the future. When I speak to groups of Canadian women, especially young Canadian women and girls, I ask them to go out and to raise their sights, to go for the good jobs and not to settle for second best. Today I am telling Canadian business, labour, and members of the Opposition the same thing: raise your sights, recognize that the labour market in Canada is changing and that we must treat each individual Canadian worker as a vital national asset. Men, women, older workers, young workers, minority groups, everyone, and business particularly ignores this great store of talent to its peril.

Mr. Speaker, the Government is determined to adjust the Unemployment Insurance Act to reflect the realities of today's work patterns-and the equity provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
With this in mind, we are proposing that 15 weeks of maternity benefits be available during the period surrounding the birth of a child, that 10 weeks of parental benefits be available to natural and adoptive parents, for either mother or father or shared between them, and that there be fewer restrictions on a claimant's ability to collect the entitlement of 15 weeks of sickness benefits.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, we are putting forward adjustments to ensure that claimants have the flexibility to draw a combination of special benefits up to a maximum of 30 weeks, that special benefits are available to claimants involved in a labour dispute, and that those who delay retirement past the age of 65 are eligible for UI benefits.
These are important adjustments, Mr. Speaker. These changes make Canada's unemployment insurance program more equitable, more flexible and more relevant to evolving social and work patterns.
Unemployment Insurance Act

The Government believes that through these measures we have taken important steps to make the UI Program more sensitive to the changing needs of Canadians. Canada is a very complex country. In some areas we have relatively high rates of unemployment, while in other areas jobs go begging for applicants. Paradoxically, even in some of the higher unemployment areas there are job vacancies because of skills shortages in that area. Clearly, facing such a challenge, there must be many approaches, not only one. That is why we rejected some of the sweeping proposals of earlier studies.
We cannot solve all of the labour market's problems in one fell swoop through government intervention. That is why we have chosen an existing mechanism-there already are training problems under the Unemployment Insurance Act-to redirect passive programs to more active uses. Even this approach has been done with moderation and with sensitivity to the needs of individual Canadians. That has been our approach all along: point people in the right direction and they will find their own way and it will lead them to a better future.
We have been accused of merely shifting people from unemployment insurance to welfare. Nothing could be further from the truth. Past experience has shown when entrance requirements for unemployment insurance have been increased-this is nothing new. The Opposition, the previous Liberal Government, did this in 1977 so do we do have some behavioural evidence-people did in fact adjust their behaviour. In the worst case, they got the extra weeks necessary to qualify for UI. In the best case, they obtained permanent and frequently better employment.
Before I close I want to talk about the financing of the Unemployment Insurance Program. In the Budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that the Government will no longer contribute funds from general revenue to the unemployment insurance account.
As I stated earlier. Governments are elected to make difficult choices. Our Government was elected to restore fiscal responsibility to the spending of Canadians' tax dollars. Years of irresponsible financing by previous Governments has meant that it is this Government that has had to make those tough choices. The Government

June 6, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
has made a commitment that it will be there to ensure that the funds do not run into a deficit position. I would like to remind Hon. Members that government funds are tax dollars and as such the UI account has always been a fund financed by the taxpayers of Canada. That is not changing.
We recognize that Canadians want to work and we are doing something positive and constructive about it. Since we were elected in 1984, 1.4 million more Canadians are working. We do not have to take a back-seat to anyone, particularly the opposition Parties, on this subject. Clearly, the best income security for any Canadian worker is a job, and the second best form of income security is the wherewithal, the skills, and the training necessary to obtain those jobs.
Income support is very important. We recognize that, but we must return to the principle that it is a temporary measure rather than a permanent remedy. In fact a fundamental principle of our strategy is to establish a continuum of programs and services for unemployed and employed Canadians that link income support, employment services, federal Government labour-market programs and skill development initiatives and bring in the provinces and labour and business in providing the solutions. These are necessary steps to help meet all the needs of a changing labour-market, the needs of current workers, of employers and of those Canadians wishing to find a productive place in our labour market. The status quo is no longer an option. In fact, the status quo does not even exist. The competitive challenges Canada faces in this world are real and they demand a co-operative response which mobilizes all of our resources and all of our talents.

To continue to grow and prosper in the 1990s and beyond, Canada needs a dynamic, flexible and highly skilled workforce. Individual Canadians need to know that they have a productive role to play that will produce a better life for them.
I am continuing to consult business, industry, labour and the various provincial governments about how we can best prepare Canadians for the changes to come.
Your input, and your cooperation, are essential if Canada is to build on our recent economic growth and achieve our great national objectives.

By working together now in this Chamber and with the other groups that I have mentioned, we will ensure that Canada is poised to take advantage of a future of unprecedented opportunity and to meet those objectives that I have talked about before, the objectives of competition, confidence, strength, compassion and sovereignty.
I look forward to the study and timely passage of Bill C-21 so Canadians can benefit from these very positive initiatives.

Mr. Speaker, the principal purpose of this Bill, the legislation which is before us, is to massively cut back on our unemployment insurance system, a system which has served Canadians well since it was introduced in 1940 following the great depression of the 1930s. In 1940, the unemployment insurance program was introduced by the Liberal Government of Mackenzie King in the aftermath of a depression where thousands and thousands of Canadians were unemployed and had no unemployment insurance, very little social assistance and had to rely on breadlines and soup kitchens which, by the way, seems to be a trademark of Tory Governments because they are back with us again in many parts of this country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, that program was introduced to make sure that Canadians, unemployed against their will, had enough money to pay their rent, buy their food and take care of their children. Since that time, it has been improved on two main occasions, in 1955 and again in 1971.
The principal goal and purpose of Bill C-21 is to cut back on that program. The reasons seem to be threefold. First, the Government is using the unemployment insurance program and the cuts that it is proposing today to cut back on the deficit. We agree that the deficit has to be dealt with, but never on the backs of the unemployed,
June 6, 1989

the people who are less capable of paying for such a huge cut. That is obviously one of the goals of the Government in introducing this Bill, to deal with their deficitcutting program.
Another obvious reason for this Bill is the Government's goal to create a level playing field to facilitate the implementation of the Free Trade Agreement. We warned Canadians during the election campaign that the Government would try to cut social programs to create this level playing field with the United States in order to create conditions so that Canadian businesses would be able to compete on a more even footing with American companies which are now allowed to come into this country without tariffs. We said that they would cut programs or the companies would move to the United States or threaten to move to the United States, and that is what is happening with this Bill and other Bills like it.
Finally, I believe the third reason which was alluded to by the Minister in her remarks, is based on a real Conservative philosophy that a progressive unemployment insurance system encourages laziness, that it makes it difficult for employers to find workers. Let us look at the record in this respect. If we look at the countries of the world with the most advanced, the most progressive unemployment insurance systems, it is in those countries that we have the lowest rates of unemployment. If we look at Sweden, Switzerland, West Germany, France, Austria, all countries with progressive, advanced unemployment insurance systems, they have very low rates of employment. All those countries, Sweden, Austria, Switzerland, have rates of unemployment less than 5 per cent.
In Canada, from 1965 to 1980 over a period of 15 years under Liberal Governments, the average rate of unemployment was 5.6 per cent. We had what I would call an excellent system for unemployment insurance. Therefore, it is a myth, a fallacy that just because we have sound social programs, sound and advanced systems of unemployment insurance, that we encourage laziness and make it difficult for employers to find workers. Sure, there are a certain number of cheaters, and I will refer to that in a minute. Sure, Canadian workers will not take jobs of poor quality, low wages, jobs where there are no unions and where there are poor working conditions which some employers, not all, would like them to do. The Government would like to make it so hard and
Unemployment Insurance Act
difficult for the unemployed that they would take those jobs. We will not support that.
Very briefly let me refer to the figures that were given to me by the Department of Employment and Immigration with respect to cheaters. In the period 1987-1988,1 am told that there were 5,507 claimants under the unemployment insurance system who were caught cheating on their unemployment insurance. That is 5,507 out of a total number of beneficiaries amounting to 2.4 million. That means that the number of cheaters was 0.2 per cent of the total number of beneficiaries under the system in that year, a very low number.
If we also look at the figures on those who lost their benefits because they refused a job, there were 6,215 who refused a job and therefore lost their benefits. Again this is out of 2.4 million beneficiaries which means that 0.25 per cent were disentitled because they refused a job. Those figures indicate that the vast majority of Canadians want to work. The main reason that they go on unemployment insurance is because they are put out of work against their will. They need that money to help them get along until a new job is given to them, to help them support their families, to buy their groceries, to pay their rent or their mortgage.
The House should know that in the Unemployment Insurance Act as it already exists, in order to collect unemployment insurance you must be ready and available to work. That is in Sections 25 and 55. It is in the legislation that you must register with a Canadian employment centre to make yourself available for work. It is in the legislation that you must accept interviews, in Sections 40 and 107, that you must accept an available job if it is a suitable job in your area of work. The legislation already requires that. Therefore, there is no evidence that unemployment insurance creates laziness and cheaters. It is true that we have a small percentage of cheaters and a small percentage of people who refuse to work, but they are less than 1 per cent of the total number of claimants under the fund.
I want to refer briefly to that history. The reason for this program, and the reason it was improved in 1955 and 1971, always by Liberal Governments, was based on the horrible experience Canadians had with the great depression of the 1930s. it should be pointed out that not only does a sound and progressive unemployment insurance system help workers when they are unemployed, it

June 6, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
also helps the economy and prevents a depression from growing deeper.
In the 1930s when a plant closed in a particular community and the workers were put out of work without any unemployment insurance, it was not long until they stopped buying groceries, stopped paying their bills and stopped paying their rent. There was a snowball effect and more industries went in the hole in that community.
By having a sound and progressive system of unemployment insurance, we make sure that the lay-offs and the closing of firms does not snowball into a deepening and widening recession. The people who are receiving the unemployment insurance spend every cent of that money when they are unemployed. They do not go to Florida, put it in the bank or under the mattress, they spend it to survive. That money goes back into the community and helps other businesses. The program is not only sound for the individual who is unemployed, but also for the community.
I want to describe how the moneys in unemployment insurance help some of the less developed provinces. In 1988, Newfoundland workers paid $169 million into the fund but collected $670 million. A lot more money went back into Newfoundland because of the unemployment situation there than the workers in that province paid into it.
In Prince Edward Island, workers paid $39 million into the fund and collected $138.5 million. Quebecers paid $2.7 billion into the fund in Quebec and collected $3.3 billion in benefits. Those moneys have flowed into those provinces and kept the basic economy of those provinces going despite high rates of unemployment in certain sectors.
The record will show that in six provinces more money has flowed into those provinces in unemployment insurance funds than has been paid into the fund by the workers. It is only in the Provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta that last year more was paid in than they received in benefits. I point that out because that will change as a result of the cuts proposed by the Minister in this Bill. Less money will go into the underdeveloped provinces than has gone in until now.
According to the changes put forward in this Bill, Canadian workers will pay more into the unemployment insurance program and get less in the form of benefits. In addition, because the Government is eliminating its legislative contribution to the fund, employers and employees will pay more in contributions once again.
I want to give a few examples to the House of what the results of these changes will be. Under the changes in Bill C-21, it will be more difficult for Canadian workers to qualify for unemployment insurance. Once they qualify they will be covered for shorter periods of time.
Let us look at some of the examples as a result of these changes. In St. John's, Newfoundland, where 10 weeks of work are required to qualify for unemployment insurance, under this legislation 14 weeks of work will be required in order to qualify. In Halifax, Nova Scotia, where 12 weeks of work was required to qualify, 18 weeks of work will be required to qualify. These are not areas known for their wealth.
In Saint John, New Brunswick, where 10 weeks of work were needed to qualify, 15 weeks of work will be required to qualify. In Quebec City, where one needed 12 weeks of work to qualify, one will now require 18 weeks of work to qualify. In Montreal, 10 weeks of work were required to qualify. Now 16 weeks of work are required in order to qualify.
In Ottawa one needed 14 weeks of work to qualify. One will now require 20 weeks to qualify. In Sudbury where 12 weeks was required, it is now 18 weeks. It is the same in Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Edmonton and Vancouver. There are very few communities in Canada where the qualification period will not be more difficult.
The same is true with respect to the duration of benefits. The duration of benefits in St. John's, Newfoundland, is changed from a minimum of 40 weeks to a maximum of 50 weeks, to a minimum of 33 weeks to a maximum of 50 weeks. In Halifax the duration goes from 28 weeks to 21 weeks; in Saint John it is from 36 weeks to 30 weeks.
Again, I could demonstrate for the record that the duration of benefits for most communities in Canada is shorter as a result of this Bill.

Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the number of Canadians who are excluded from full benefits under the UI Program because in the view of the bureaucracy within the Unemployment Insurance Commission they have committed some type of a dishonest act and have quit without reason. We can be certain from the amount of evidence available that if those people had an advocate they would be receiving benefits as well. The whole claim by the Government that there are cheaters is spurious from the very beginning.
The Government has claimed to find approximately $1.29 billion from the four methods it has used to

capture this money: the longer qualification time; shorter duration of receiving the benefits; penalizing people who quit, according to the Government, unfairly; and when the Government prosecutes people, and saving money in that manner.
The Government upbraids the private sector for not spending enough money on training in Canada. Approximately 25 per cent of the private sector in Canada does train. I would suggest that we do not need to be talking about all the training that will happen under the changes to the unemployment insurance program if the private sector did the type of training that it ought to have been doing all along. As I said, $1.4 billion is the amount of money the private sector spends on training.
Through these changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, the federal Government has captured very nearly $1.4 billion from the workers of the private sector. In effect it has added a tax on the worker insofar as they are receiving less benefits. If you do not get the money, it does not come, it does not accrue to you and it is money that you do not have. If it is the Government that takes it away from you, I think it quite legitimately can be called a tax. The Government has forced on to the workers an amount of money equivalent to what the whole private sector spends on training and it has said, hey, this is what we are going to use for training, we have such a wonderful gift for you.
I think we ought to be emphasizing here that the majority of training really ought to be taking place within the larger corporations in our society. As a matter of fact, within my experience, I know that a goodly portion of the training really takes place in small business, with small contractors. More often than not the large multinationals or the larger Canadian corporations suck up these training people at the expense of small business which is not able to afford that kind of a drain on its earning power.
There are four or five programs which I believe the Minister ought to have come clean about and said: "Listen, since the Budget, these things are no longer relevant. It might be nice for us to be able to talk about them in Parliament, but they really do not have any claim on the unemployment insurance funds and, therefore, are irrelevant to this discussion."
Unemployment Insurance Act
I would have thought that the Minister at least would have had the decency not to refer to the entry level skill jobs where she was talking about co-op training. Co-op training occurs in high schools. There is no way that a high school student is going to be able to amass enough unemployment insurance credits to be able to draw on the unemployment insurance fund. I cannot understand why the Minister would be making reference to that kind of training at all when the Bill is supposed to be talking about changes to the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
I would repeat, as the speaker before me has done, that it would be foolish for me as an individual, as someone who has been a worker all my life, as a Member of the New Democratic Party to stand here and say that we are opposed to training. What we have here are two different subjects. One is unemployment insurance which is to protect people when they become unemployed. This Government must be very fond of unemployed people because it sure has created enough of them. The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) is absolutely right. Unemployment still has not risen to the level of the pre-recession level. The Government makes a lot of claims about the growth in the Canadian economy, but when you start from so low, even the 4 per cent that they claim does not really amount to very much. The Government ought to recognize that and confess it.
The Community Futures Program is a similar program. It should not have been included here. By definition social assistance recipients are not eligible to receive unemployment insurance. The reference to social assistance recipients in this context is abhorrent to us. I know it happened back in the Province of Saskatchewan. What we are really talking about is work for welfare, and the federal Government should not be involved in that kind of a scheme. It is something which borders so closely on enforced slavery that it is not something that the Government of this country should be involved in.
With reference to self-employment and entrepreneurship, can you imagine, the Government is bringing in legislation that is going to allow unemployed people to be able to take out lump sums of money in order to start businesses. I would suspect that most young people who become unemployed are totally unaware that 90 per cent of all new businesses fail within the first year. A federal Government should not be involved in a scheme that gives money to an unemployed person in the hope that

June 6, 1989
Transportation Safety
they will be able to start a business. Maybe they are trying to make them think that they will be able to start a bank.
I saw in the paper on the weekend that the bank profits are up again. That is certainly not much of a surprise. Maybe these young people are going to receive assistance to form a bank. If that is the case, they probably will do well, but I suspect the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and a few others might have a few words to say about that.
It is a mystery to me how the Government can make claims as it does that these things are part of the unemployment assistance program. With regard to the industrial assistance program that is in place, I found out from the Government today that indeed it will continue to put in its portion. However, unemployed people, when they now go to take courses, will have their tuition paid for out of the unemployment insurance fund. This whole program is nothing more than a scam by this Government in order to privatize the unemployment insurance system, in order to privatize the training within the country.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy brought in in 1985 has proven to be nothing more than that. The numbers available on it are atrocious. I would like to give an example of one of the Canadian Jobs Strategy Programs in Peterborough, Ontario which states that a good example of the fly-by-night training resulting from the Tory strategy occurred in Peterborough, Ontario. After cutting back on purchases of space at Sir Sandford Fleming Community College, a $340,000 contract was given to the newly created Gowrie Computer Systems to train 50 people in computer skills.
I certainly have discovered that computer skills among the Canadian Jobs Strategy proponents in the Government seems to be very high on the list. We find that after a one-shot course, the company's training work was finished, but they still got to keep $100,000 worth of computer equipment purchased with CEIC money, and meanwhile the computer facilities at the community college have been allowed to deteriorate.
This epitomizes the problem which we are facing with these changes to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I cannot do anything but vote against this motion.
