subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSPORTATION SAFETY INCREASED FUNDING FOR SAFETY INSPECTORS
PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSPORTATION SAFETY INCREASED FUNDING FOR SAFETY INSPECTORS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of increasing funding for transportation safety inspectors.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to bring forth this motion today, particularly on behalf of my colleague, the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), who is presently busy in the Transport Committee on a matter not totally unrelated to the subject matter of this motion.
Safety is always an important concern, especially with regard to the transportation industry. I suspect that in the minds of most Canadians and Members of the House it is even more important when it comes to the matter of airline safety.
The subject matter of the motion before us is that in the opinion of the House, the Government should consider the advisability of increasing funding for transportation safety inspectors. That is rather a broad motion that could cover air, marine, long-distance interprovincial hauling by truck and other modes, and rail. I believe the main thrust of the remarks this evening will be related to the airline industry.

Most Canadians and Members of the House perceive a real problem in safety and safety inspections throughout the airline industry in Canada. We have all been only too familiar with the many stories about near misses and the increasing concern by the travelling public and those associated with the industry directly about safety with transportation and what appears to be a deteriorating standard of safety inspection. This has taken place over the past number of years, beyond the terms of any one government, and has been creating a considerable state of concern within the body politic.
In studying this complicated question of transportation safety, particularly air safety, I want to begin by talking about deregulation and its increased stresses on the transportation industry. The deregulation of the transportation industry, begun by the Liberal Government in 1983 and continued by the Conservative Governments since that time, operates under the theory that increased competition is good for the travelling public. Undoubtedly there may be cases where that is so, but there are problems.
One problem with deregulation is that it allows a number of smaller carriers into the industry. Again, while that may be good in some instances, it also creates problems particularly in the area of safety and inspection.
For example, let us look at the air passenger industry. Previously, the vast majority of air travel was handled by the big three: Air Canada, Canadian Airlines and Ward-air. These airlines tended to police themselves with self-inspection and random checks by Department of Transport employees on safety regulations. These DOT inspectors were assigned to work with the major airlines on site. That was their prime mandate in the past, and is quite different from the work they are required to perform now.
Two things have happened since deregulation. First, the big three have become the big two, and there has been a proliferation of smaller, short distance airlines.
It is to be assumed that the big two are still operating under the old system of self-policing and random checks by DOT officials. The problem occurs with the smaller airlines and smaller aircraft. They are often small operations with less than 10 aircraft, aircraft which tend to be hand-me-downs discarded by the majors both nationally and internationally.
Transportation Safety
Second, these smaller companies do not have the qualified personnel nor the cash to pay to have these qualified personnel on staff as maintenance workers.
Third, they are operating in the hub and spoke system, which means that many smaller aircraft are flying into the major airports like Toronto, Vancouver and Edmonton, where passengers are transferred to the major airlines for long distances. This means that there are more aircraft with more parts, and more varied parts, flying more often.
For example, where a major carrier used to fly a 747 carrying some 400 passengers once a day, a small feeder airline will fly a Dash-8 with 20 passengers five times a day.
I am the Member for an area with an airport that is both famous and infamous to many Members of the House, past and present. Castlegar Airport used to have one or two flights a day, with fairly large passenger jets carrying a significant number of passengers. Now there are some four or five flights a day, almost every day, by two different airlines. In addition, there is a small regional airport that also serves as a training base for a pilots' school operated in conjunction with a community college. The number of flights going in and out of what until recently was the airport with the least proportion of successful landings and take-offs in the western hemisphere, has created more than a normal share of problems in terms of safety.
Luckily, and largely due to the skill and dedication of the people employed in and around the industry, to my knowledge there have not been any near misses or serious incidents. We are thankful for that, but unless there are improvements other airports in similar situations to ours may find themselves running out of time and luck. I hope not.
As a result of deregulation there are more flights on feeder routes and more flights into minor airports without state of the art technology and often in veiy difficult locations.
There are more take-offs and landings per hour of aircraft operation. Those familiar with the industry will know that it is during the take-offs and landings that serious incidents are more likely to occur.
There are also more people travelling as a result of deregulated prices. That has been one of the benefits of deregulation. The locations are much busier.

June 6, 1989
Transportation Safety
During this process the number of inspectors have been dropping due to budget cuts. In a recent article on April 14 in the Times-Transcript of Moncton, New Brunswick, Dick Peters, chairman of the Aircraft Operations Group Association, said that Budget cut-backs and insufficient staffing levels make it difficult for staff inspectors of the Department to keep up with changes in the industry.
The association represents some 440 civil aviation inspectors.
I want to quote from this article. The headline states: "Budget cuts creating unsafe airline industry?". The article states:
"The skies won't be safer unless the federal Government begins keeping pace with changes in the airline industry", a spokesman for civil aviation inspectors said Thursday.
R.A. Peters, chairman of the Aircraft Operations Group Association, said budget cut-backs and insufficient staffing levels make it difficult for inspectors to keep up with changes in the industry.
"Nothing has changed," said Peters, noting his predecessor made similar comments in an interview here last year.
"In fact, it's gotten worse."
Peters, whose association represents about 440 civil aviation inspectors, says insufficient salary levels also means many of their numbers are also being hired away by private industry.
There are some Members, I am sure, who are going to say that this is obviously a self-serving statement. To some extent, it possibly is. However, it does not alter the facts of the situation that the salary levels are far below other areas and are not sufficient to keep the very highly qualified people they must have in order to do their job. It is an important job.
Peters pointed out a recently leaked memorandum that confirmed inspector workload in the large aircraft field has increased 400 per cent and yet the numbers of inspectors have declined by 50 per cent.
How many of us would put up with that kind of situation in our own line of work, whether it is in this House or elsewhere? Maybe we would put up with it here, because nobody drafts us for this job. In the case of most Canadians, they would find a situation intolerable where there was a workload increase of 400 per cent and a reduced workforce, down by half.
To go back to the story:
"Numbers have declined partly to attrition but also because we're not attracting people from the military any more," said Peters.
He said trained aviators from the armed forces either re-enlist or are hired by private airlines.
Peters explained civil aviation inspectors must be as well trained as pilots because they must regulate the industry.
However, low staff levels means training time is increasingly difficult to come by.
"In Tbronto at Pearson Airport, some inspectors haven't been on training courses for four to eight months" he said.
"If we don't keep up with the industry, we'll start losing credibility and our ability to assess the industry," he said.
Working conditions and salaries just aren't attracting new inspectors. "In order to be an inspector, you have to be as qualified as a pilot, and our inspectors are going out the door like you wouldn't believe," he said.
Inspectors earn about 50 per cent less than an average airline pilot, Peters estimated.
"The gap in salaries must become a more realistic one", he said, pointing to the situation in Great Britain -
In Maggie Thatcher's Great Britain, in fact-
"-where inspectors automatically earn two-thirds the salary of a British Airways captain".
I hope the Government will listen to that because we have to bring these salaries more into line with the situation in other countries in order to keep and attract the best possible people. Nobody can argue that we need the very best people when it comes to this kind of occupation, where lives are at stake.
"With the public's increasing concern on health and safety", said Peters, "the government would be wise to ensure safety standards are maintained in the skies.
The industry", he said, "is not capable of auditing itself. "We need an adequate third party to ensure federal standards are met."
Surely, Members on the other side of the House and all Members will want to ensure that the standards that we do have, whether they are fully adequate or otherwise-and we hope that they are-that at least those standards that we do have are met. I am sure that will not be argued by anybody.
I just want to quote briefly another story from the Toronto Star of May 27 of this year, entitled: "Union says safety may be threatened by shortage of federal pilot inspectors". It largely draws on the same sources but a number of the facts and figures are different.
A shortage of pilot inspectors may threaten air safety, their union warns.
June 6, 1989

The federal Transport Department may be forced to have airlines
inspect themselves, leading to a possible drop in standards-
They state that:
-an airline employed inspector may pass unqualified pilots to please management. He's liable to come under pressure from management. After all, where does the employees' allegiance lie?
I think all Members here recognize that that may be the case. It is why we go to great pains in a variety of agencies, whether they deal with occupational health and safety or public health and safety, or many other areas of jurisdiction, to ensure that there are two-party or tripartite boards which represent a number of different constituencies so that the public will know or feel secure in the knowledge that those decisions are made not by someone with a gun to their head, directly or indirectly, but by somebody who knows what they are doing and whose only duty is to the travelling public.
"Large numbers of senior pilots are due to retire", Peters said. One airline that Peters refused to name faces 700 inspections next year so its pilots can fly newly introduced aircraft, move from one aircraft to another and move up to captain from first officer.
Seven hundred inspections next year in just one airline.
"This is where the benefits of an independent checking system get thrown out of the window- There are 180 vacancies in the transport department's pilot and pilot inspector group", he said, "and management has made little effort to fill them".
A transport department official said the shortage is smaller than Peters claims and the Department does not expect to let airlines do inspections.
But Roger Burgess-Webb, a spokesman for the Canadian Airline Pilots Association, agreed that the inspector shortage could lead to declining standards, particularly on smaller airlines.
"The pilots association believes the Transport Department, which sets the standards for pilots, should accept the responsibility to enforce them", Burgess-Webb said.
I might add that the Canadian Airline Pilots Association has a great deal of credibility. If any one hedges, usually on the side of caution in making statements that seem alarmist, it is certainly not the Canadian Airline Pilots Association. They tend, and understandably so, to be very defensive of their role and their own right to refuse to fly aircraft that they deem to be unsafe. If they
Transportation Safety
are alarmed, I suggest there should be more than a little concern amongst the rest of us.
My colleague for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) spoke with Mr. Peters just the other day regarding one of the memoranda mentioned in the article. He says that he has just done a tour of airports out West and it is "chaotic" out there. Inspectors are leaving daily, 10 this month and 30 or so next month. That is alarming, considering the drop in inspectors we have already had. If we are continuing to see this kind of demise of an occupational group upon which so much depends, we have to be more than a little alarmed and concerned.
To wrap up this point in brief, there is increasing workload, a decreasing number of inspectors, less time available for training to keep up with new technology.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the matter of Bill C-2, an Act to create the Transportation Accident Investigation Board: This Board is going to amalgamate accident investigations presently carried out under the various air, marine, rail and commodity pipeline boards. Because of the possibly expanded scope of the new board, to include such areas as passenger boating, there will be a need for more safety inspectors for this board to function well.
The reduction of inspection staff is further complicated by this Government's decision to replace the Canadian Aviation Safety Board and other transport safety inspection agencies with one super board. I think that does not need much explanation. However, there is a story here dated May 19, 1989, in the Ottawa Citizen which, in quoting a number of sources including the Pilots Association, it says:
-warned that the proposed new board would lack the expertise to properly investigate air accidents and would likely degenerate into the internal problems that plagued the safety board.
Some board members obviously felt their investigators were not pursuing enough leads before. That I suspect, Mr. Speaker, is probably due to the fact that there were not enough of them. That is what the motion before us is all about.
The Pilots Association recommended that the government retain an exclusive aviation safety board and not submerge it in an agency that investigates a broad range of transportation accidents.
There is enough in what was said and directly quoted by those most intimately concerned with the inspection of air safety people in this country to realize that we have a problem on our hands. The Government has acknowl-

Transportation Safety
edged that there is a serious problem and that there has been a serious backlog in terms of staffing levels. We must begin to make changes now that will ensure we pay appropriate levels of salaries, that we get enough people with the experience to do the required job if flying and other methods of transportation in Canada are to be as safe as the public has the right to expect them to be.
I support the motion and ask that other Parties in the House give it their support as well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSPORTATION SAFETY INCREASED FUNDING FOR SAFETY INSPECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to address the House on the important issue raised by the Hon. Member for Kootenay West-Revels-toke (Mr. Kristiansen) on behalf of his seat-mate, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), namely the adequacy of the present level of funding for transportation safety inspection.
I want to thank my hon. friends for the opportunity to set the record straight once and for all. Transport Canada employs some 550 federal civil aviation, airworthiness, passenger safety and dangerous goods inspectors and others who have had day-to-day responsibility for ensuring air safety. These people are recruited into Transport Canada as highly qualified professionals in their respective medium. They then undergo training for up to a year to become fully qualified. Their jobs and responsibilities are as diverse as the aviation industry itself, but Transport Canada has ensured that aviation regulation staff numbers and the qualifications they bring to their respective jobs are adequate to meet the increasing demands brought about by rapid expansion and restructuring of the aviation industry.
Air-worthiness inspectors verify that civil aircraft are in compliance with air-worthiness standards by inspecting companies for adherence to regulations and by inspecting aircraft to determine that safety standards are met. Inspectors also examine and licence aircraft maintenance engineers and approve maintenance manuals and procedures for all air carriers. They collect and analyze data related to aircraft defects and take corrective action where necessary.
Since 1986-87, the number of air carrier inspectors grew to 137 from 102 across Canada. In 1988-89, 29 of these inspectors oversaw large air carrier operations. Air carrier inspectors conduct initial and continuing inspections of air carrier operations, air crew and facilities.
The number of dangerous goods inspectors in the aviation sector has increased to 15 from 9 since 1986-87. Dangerous goods inspectors conduct on-site inspections of all air carriers to ensure the safe transportation of dangerous goods by Canadian and foreign aircraft operating in Canadian air space.
The number of person-years in the passenger safety inspection activity increased to 16 from 11 in recent years. These inspectors conduct inspections of air carrier passenger operations, cabin attendant training courses and perform audits to ensure compliance with regulations.
Staff in the inspector engineering training section of the aviation group develop training courses and provide training to all the departments' civil aviation inspectors, air-worthiness technical inspectors and air-worthiness engineers to ensure they are fully qualified.
Transport Canada's licensing inspectors, 112 in number, conduct flight tests associated with the issue and endorsement of aviation personnel licences. They also monitor and inspect the activities of flight training staff and organizations, corporate passenger aircraft and special aviation events. Industry personnel who exercise licensing authority on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) are monitored by these inspectors. They also develop and implement policies and standards for the licensing of aviation personnel such as pilots, aircraft maintenance engineers and air traffic controllers and for the registration of aircraft.
The need for comprehensive investigations relating to air carrier operations and air-worthiness infractions resulted in ten more person-years being added to the aviation enforcement section of Transport Canada. The unit which employs 48 is responsible for preventing, detecting, investigating and processing infractions of the Aeronautics Act, air regulations and air navigation orders. This includes the preparation and preservation of court cases before the Civil Aviation Tribunal and the application of regulations addressing occupational safety
June 6, 1989

and health of crew members aboard aircraft. They also are responsible for developing national policy, procedures and training for maintaining functional control of the aviation enforcement organization.
The inspector workforce in the aviation safety programs unit has increased to 17 in 1988-89 from 12.5 person-years in 1986-87. Inspectors in this component conduct accident prevention programs for commercial aviation, the Civil Air Search and Rescue Association, private and recreational aviation, as well as passenger safety education. They also conduct confidential safety surveys, company aviation safety officer courses and aviation safety briefings.
There are 31 inspectors in the Aviation Regulation Directorate who are not directly available for inspection duties. These inspectors are managers who are responsible for ensuring inspection responsibilities are carried out in accordance with departmental policies, procedures and standards.
While my preceding remarks have discussed the 550 inspector resources, there is a total of 900-plus employees engaged in regulatory activities. Further, the aviation group of Transport Canada, whose principal mandate is aviation safety, number some 7,000 employees.
These human resources are supported by an excellent aviation navigation system that has been developed over many years and is continually improved and modernized to take advantage of new technology and to meet the changing need of the air transportation system. In Canada and world-wide, air navigation systems exist to prevent aircraft from colliding with one another. Transport Canada has a mandate to reduce the threat of mid-air collisions and in fact has recently set up a mid-air collision avoidance committee. It is now studying a number of proposals it has received from other groups on this issue.
The Department also asked for public comment from the aviation community last year. At this moment, it is studying all the comments received.
The Department will also develop policies on technical equipment designed to avoid airborne collisions through the use of what are termed Mode C and Mode S transponders. It is expected that within three years, most Canadian carriers will have equipped their aircraft with these traffic alert collision avoidance systems.
Transportation Safety
It should be mentioned at this point that Transport Canada last fall organized a conference in Ottawa on collision avoidance agencies to exchange ideas and information. Many of the participants were given airborne flight demonstrations to see how the systems worked. The reaction was most optimistic.
For the past several years, the microwave landing system project that involves replacing and improving current systems that are used in guiding aircraft during approaches and landings has been under way. The new MLS will be much more accurate and reliable in determining the flight path to a runway. Approximately 150 such systems will be installed right up to the year 2000. A number of private organizations have purchased MLS units, and Transport Canada's specialists are installing them and helping with instrument design.
Transport Canada is constantly looking for ways to improve its services to the flying community through its flight services stations. Recently, improvements have been made by the provision of new electronic displays and storage of aeronautical information, pilot self-briefing systems and automated weather observation services. Transport Canada is also testing an automated system that displays meteorological and other operational data for pilots. It is known as MIDS or Multi-purpose Information Display System. Four stations in the Arctic are using earlier versions and so are five sites in Ontario. Within a few years, it is expected that about 100 new MIDS units will be in operation.
Another major modernization program currently under way and expected to be completed within the next two or three years is the RAMP Program. This is one that will re-equip all major radar sites across the country with more sophisticated technology. This kind of equipment does not come cheap. The total cost is estimated to be close to $800 million. The team that got this project under way was formed early in the 1980s. Its task was to produce and install 24 primary and secondary surveillance radar systems, along with 17 independent secondary radar systems, plus 29 display and data processing systems at various locations across Canada.

June 6, 1989
Transportation Safety
New radar systems have been installed at Ottawa and at Transport Canada's training institute in Cornwall, Ontario. There are other systems at sites in Hamilton and Goose Bay, Newfoundland. Installation work has started at other sites in Sept-Iles, London, Calgary and Victoria. A new system goes into operation at Toronto this fall and others will follow in due course across the country.
My time has run out but there are other things, Mr. Speaker. There is a CAAT system, the Canadian Automatic Air Traffic System. It is a major Crown project which has become a focus for air traffic control modernization. It will produce extensive automation for handling of flight data and the use of common controller work stations. Transport Canada is now evaluating two requests for proposals that were released to the industry in September, 1988.
Incidentally, many of the projects I have outlined represent only a part of the Canadian Airport Systems Plan or CASP which is Transport Canada's approach to the modernization and restoration of the technical infrastructure of the country's air navigation system. This is a strategy for an evolutionary development of the technical infrastructure into the 21st century.
I could go on but I see time has taken over, Mr. Speaker, so I rest my case.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSPORTATION SAFETY INCREASED FUNDING FOR SAFETY INSPECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak during Private Member's Business to motion M-272, tabled on April 4, 1989 by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus), which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should
consider the advisability on increasing funding for transportation
safety inspectors.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to provide an overview of Transport Canada's programs for the maintenance and improvement of aviation safety in Canada. Transport Canada has established a company aviation safety management program. This innovative program is free and is designed to help companies with risk management. The
program has three components, which include an executive safety seminar, a company aviation safety officer course and a follow-up service provided by Transport Canada's regional aviation safety officers.
The seminar was launched in 1987 in the Aviation Group's six regions. The purpose of the seminar is to motivate and encourage company chief executive officers to establish and maintain a safety program within their companies. This approach has proved to be very effective, and a number of executives have already taken steps to set up programs of this kind. The course designed for company aviation safety officers has existed for many years. In 1987, course content was restructured to adjust to changing needs. The course is designed to teach officers or representatives of company chief executive officers methods for risk management within their own companies. Regional personnel responsible for the aviation safety program offers one course per year. Between 30 and 50 people participate, depending on the region.
In the same program, the regional aviation safety adviser offers a follow-up service whose main objective is to ensure the continued existence and effectiveness of company aviation safety programs. Basically, the overall objective of the company aviation safety management program is to help companies help themselves.
There is irrefutable evidence that this type of program is profitable for the airlines. It helps save lives and keep aircraft in good condition. It is one more way of providing Canadians with a safe and efficient air transportation system.
Mr. Speaker, the company aviation safety management program is only one of many accident prevention programs that regional aviation safety officers offer directly to the industry. New programs are being designed daily.
International experts on aircraft accident prevention have confirmed tht at least 80 per cent of aircraft accidents are the result of human actions or the absence thereof. The remaining 20 per cent are attributed to flight equipment and atmospheric conditions. Pilot decision-making is involved in and determines the majority of accidents in the human factor group.
June 6, 1989

To reduce human error, a new program was made available to all pilots in 1987. The pilot decion-making program is the result of joint efforts by American, French and Canadian civil aviation authorities.
A decision-making course has also been incorporated in the Canadian program for student pilot training. This part of the program will be directed by the services responsible for Canadian aviation regulations. Decisionmaking workshops conducted by regional aviation safety officers in all regions of the Aviation Group are offered to pilots.
In preparing these workshops, experts on safety awareness reviewed reports on specific aircraft accidents and incidents and the reports on occurrences drafted by the Canadian Aviation Safety Board.
Mr. Speaker, Transport Canada's aviation safety programs also acknowledge the important role of education.
In Canada, over 70,000 licensed pilots receive the Aviation Safety Letter six times a year, as well as the changes published in the Transport Canada aviation information bulletin. Every year, Transport Canada receives positive comments on its news bulletin.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, Transport Canada will produce and publish about 1,600 publications on aviation this year. Among these publications, the Aviation Safety Letter has the widest circulation and the largest number of readers. It is read by pilots, operators, mechanics, air traffic controllers and the industry. It is even read by experts in other countries who use the information in the news letter in their own aviation safety services. This publication even gives information obtained from foreign air safety services that can be useful to Canadian pilots.
Transport Canada's national verification program is a key and essential strategy for performing the Department's duties and ensuring an adequate level of service to the aviation community and users of air services. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSPORTATION SAFETY INCREASED FUNDING FOR SAFETY INSPECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comments are directed toward safety inspection in the marine sector. First let me state that this Government is dedicated to the development and operation of an efficient and safe national marine transportation system. This mandate is a prime responsibility of the Canadian Coast Guard.
In discharging this responsibility, the Coast Guard operates in a demanding environment. First, economic and technological advancements have expanded both the scope and complexity of the Coast Guard work in marine safety matters in recent years. Larger and more technologically complex vessels pose new challenges to marine regulators. The Canadian Coast Guard continues to work in this regard toward improved safety in the marine environment.
The marine surveyors of the Ship Safety Branch of the Coast Guard assume many of the tasks associated with responding to recommendations from investigations and inquiries following any major marine accident. In the course of their analysis, existing safety regulations and standards are thoroughly reviewed. Revisions are incorporated to be certain that prevention of marine accidents is improved.
The Ship Safety Branch administers, on behalf of the Minister of Transport, those parts of the Canada Shipping Act involving all aspects of the programs for ship safety and ship-source pollution.

June 6, 1989
Transportation Safety
In order to achieve this objective, approximately 310 inspectors, including professional management staff, are located across the Dominion of Canada providing services from six regional offices and overseeing 30 district offices distributed from Newfoundland to British Columbia, including the Canadian Arctic.
All of these offices receive guidance on the application of the Canada Shipping Act and other pertinent legislation from Ship Safety headquarters located in Ottawa. The distribution of human resources reflects the level of activity in each area.
In order to ensure a safe marine transportation system, Coast Guard marine regulatory activities include development and enforcement of marine regulations for Canadian and foreign ships visiting Canadian ports; assessment and design approval of all commercial ships to ensure the adequacy of their construction; inspection and certification of these ships to ensure their safety and sea worthiness; examination and certification of marine officers and crews to ensure that ships are properly and competently manned; inspection of marine cargoes, including dangerous goods; and the registration of ships and licensing of vessels.
Under the pollution prevention function, regulations are developed and ships inspected to reduce incidents of ship-source pollution in Canadian waters and to ensure that ships satisfy international convention requirements. Investigations are also carried out to obtain evidence for prosecution purposes where ship-source pollution occurs.
I would like to take this opportunity to spell out some of the services provided by the Canadian Coast Guard designed to facilitate safe navigation of all vessels, including particularly those with potentially polluting cargoes. These remarks are particularly pertinent in the wake of the Exxon Valdez incident. I would like to provide a summary of some of the measures already in place in Canada to ensure that such an incident as the Exxon Valdez accident does not occur in Canadian waters.
These services include an extensive network of conventional and electronic aids to navigation; the broadcast of safety information by a network of Coast Guard radio stations; a system of traffic lanes and traffic separation zones in waters with significant volumes of traffic; and a
series of vessel traffic management stations which monitor and guide ships through areas of significant traffic or in areas where large volumes of potentially polluting cargo are routinely carried by ship.
In Canada, high level traffic management systems, including radar surveillance and real time communications, are provided in areas with substantial tanker traffic and similar systems with VHF radio coverage but without radar are provided in three other sites. The radar equipped sites include Placentia Bay, Newfoundland; Halifax Harbour; approaches to the Bay of Fundy and to Saint John Harbour; the areas of Les Escoumins, Quebec City, and Montreal in the St. Lawrence; the Straits of Juan de Fuca; approaches to Vancouver Harbour, B.C., and the lower west coast of Vancouver Island. Sites monitoring traffic by radio only operate in Prince Rupert, British Columbia, the Detroit-St. Clair River area and in St. John's, Newfoundland. Participation in these traffic management systems is mandatory for all vessels over 60 feet in length.
This system of traffic management centres with trained regulators and standardized procedures is among the most extensive in the world. It has been put in place specifically to reduce the risk of collision, grounding and striking accidents involving large ships, particularly where they carry potentially polluting cargoes.
In addition, Canada has established a unique system of off-shore reporting systems in which ships wishing to enter Canadian waters first file with the Coast Guard, by radio, information relating to their voyage and the condition of their vessel to ensure that it meets Canadian standards and does not pose a pollution risk.
Once entering confined waters, a comprehensive system of pilotage provided by the four Crown corporations responsible for this service ensures that a trained mariner thoroughly familiar with the local area boards each vessel to provide guidance and local expertise.
In addition to these systems designed to facilitate safe passage, Canada also has an extensive regulatory regime under which tankers must meet stringent standards of design, construction, manning and operation. In addition to these standards applying to Canadian flag vessels, Canada imposes additional requirements on foreign flag vessels beyond those already required by international convention. We require that ships of foreign registry
June 6, 1989

cany a non-Canadian ship compliance certificate to demonstrate that they meet these standards.
Current Canadian requirements regarding oil pollution prevention are contained in the oil pollution prevention regulations and non-Canadian ships compliance certificate regulations. They were both made pursuant to the Canada Shipping Act. Safety regulations regarding construction, equipment, operation, officer certification and safe manning requirements are similarly made pursuant to the Canada Shipping Act.
In addition, under the same legislation, pollution prevention officers are created and empowered to take action to prevent a pollution incident within Canadian waters or fishing zones. These powers require that a ship allow boarding and inspection by a pollution prevention officer, produce information or documents demanded by such an officer, and enter or leave certain areas as may be designated by the pollution prevention officer. This is all with a view to preventing a pollution incident or mitigating its consequences.
Notwithstanding the various systems and provisions outlined above designed to reduce the risk of a similar accident as happened in the waters of Alaska, Ministers have recently directed their deputies to carry out a thorough review of various tanker safety systems. I think that is very appropriate at this time, particularly in view of the fact that we are recognizing Environment Week in Canada.
I would like to inform this House that we are committed to safe marine transportation systems. We are confident that the present level of funding allocated for this purpose is adequate. It is something that we will continue to look at in the future to make sure that we maintain those standards.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS BUSINESS - MOTIONS   TRANSPORTATION SAFETY INCREASED FUNDING FOR SAFETY INSPECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to address the motion of the Hon. Member opposite as it applies to the work of two groups of inspectors; those dedicated to ensuring the safety of the railway system in this country and those who ensure that dangerous goods are transported safely. I would first like to put forward some historical background on the place of railway inspectors in the system.
Transportation Safety
The federal Government is responsible for the regulation of safety on much of the railway system in Canada. This responsibility has been successfully carried out by a highly qualified, professional staff ever since widespread development of railways was undertaken in this country.
For many years, regulation was performed by a regulatory agency, most recently the National Transportation Agency. The NTA, and its predecessor boards and commissions, derived powers to regulate safety from the Railway Act, one of our older and more durable pieces of legislation. Nevertheless, as Members will recall, it became increasingly clear that railway regulatory staff were burdened with outdated legal requirements which limited their powers and impeded the modernization of regulations. There was also the need to separate safety regulation from economic regulation and accident investigation.
For these and other reasons, Parliament passed the Railway Safety Act in 1988, proclaimed on January 1, 1989, making railway safety regulation a responsibility of the Minister of Transport.
The Government made it clear when the Railway Safety Act was introduced in the House that safety inspectors had been doing an excellent job. The excellent safety record of the Canadian railway industry testifies to that performance. The Government also made a commitment to strengthen railway safety by the passage of the new Act. This is being implemented as the provisions of the Railway Safety Act replace those of the old Railway Act.
First, the new Act has substantially reduced unproductive regulatory activities by removing paper burden from the inspectors. For instance, under the old legislation, regulatory orders had been issued at the rate of more than five for each working day, mostly because the Railway Act required them, not because it was in the interests of safety. Written orders are now only produced when the resolution of a safety problem cannot be agreed upon by the inspector and a railway company or other party. In other words, improved communication, backed up by the powers granted by the new Act, has replaced detailed regulation by written order.
For railway construction and alteration projects, the old legislation required inspectors to review plans, visit construction sites, issue pre-construction orders, inspect completed works and issue final approvals. The majority of these works were routine alterations, often in remote

June 6, 1989
Transportation Safety
locations, which posed no threat to safety. Field forces now are no longer forced to carry out multiple inspections and can choose sites to visit on a random basis, exercising professional judgment as to what railway works ought to be monitored.
Work is already under way on a major overhaul of the operating rules which are critical to the safety of the movement of trains. Safety inspectors can now move quickly with a minimum of bureaucratic paperwork to modify and update rules that previously were locked into the cumbersome regulatory process. This was one of the key concerns of Mr. Justice Foisy in his inquiry into the Hinton train collision.
What is the impact on railway safety? The Government has retained all the railway safety inspection resources that were available under the previous legislation. By giving the inspectors greater ability to direct resources toward the most productive safety activities, Canadians are getting more for their regulatory dollar. Both the regulator and the industry spend less time on paper-pushing exercises. The Government can focus on essential safety activities and the industry must respond.
There are 97 railway safety inspector positions in Transport Canada's Railway Safety Directorate. Inspecting staff have expertise in the three major disciplines of safety regulation: railway operations, railway equipment, and railway infrastructure. These persons are certified to enter and inspect railway premises as necessary to carry out their responsibilities. They are knowledgeable about railway rules and operating practices, about the operation and maintenance of equipment and machinery, about the construction and maintenance of railway track and structures, and train movement control systems.
The staff of 97 inspectors are located across the national railway system. There are 23 in headquarters in the National Capital region. The balance of 74 are in regional offices maintained in Moncton, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver. Each regional office has available inspectors with expertise in all aspects of railway operation and maintenance. The regulatory staff carry out a program of inspections on a continuous basis and are available to respond to requests, inquiries and complaints from local authorities, from railway employees, or from private individuals.
Persons appointed as railway safety inspectors are no longer encumbered with other duties to perform, such as accident investigation or cost arbitration. As well, the inspectors have greater powers under the new legislation than were available under the old Railway Act. Again, I point out that changes brought about by the Railway Safety Act mean that the resources, particularly the inspectors' time and talents, are better employed. We have had a tangible increase in resource-utilization because of this realignment.
The Railway Safety Act provides the inspectors with right of access to investigate anything pertinent to safe railway operations. Companies and individuals are compelled to assist the inspectors in carrying out their legitimate duties. Most important, the inspectors can intervene and take direct action where they see a threat to safety.
To an increasing extent, government inspectors are monitoring how the railway companies are performing safety-related activities and spending less time attempting to duplicate these functions themselves. Inspecting to ensure that railways are managing safety provides Canadians with effective regulation.
After three months of regulation under the new legislation, the results are positive. Inspectors have welcomed their new powers and freedom to exercise judgment. Of equal importance is the fact that the industry, both management and unions, and other involved parties, have reacted in a co-operative manner and are assisting in the development and implementation of modernized regulations, standards, and rules. Indeed, the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson) knows that the Government is monitoring the implementation of the Railway Safety Act very closely. He also knows that the measure of success will be the safety performance of the industry and the ability of our inspecting staff to influence it.
The Canadian railway system has an excellent safety record. Our goal and the goal of railway safety inspectors is to ensure that this record is preserved and improved.

I would now like to turn to a somewhat separate but nevertheless related matter. In 1985, regulations designed to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods were put into force pursuant to the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act. These regulations reduce the possibility of an accidental release of a dangerous good by requiring that all dangerous goods, as listed or defined in the regulations, be identified, be classified, be marked, be handled in an appropriate manner, be contained in approved packages, tanks, cylinders or containers, and that individuals involved in their transportation be trained with respect to both the requirements of the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act and regulations, as well as in the characteristics of the dangerous goods being moved.
The dangerous goods regulations also ensure that in the event of an accidental release of a dangerous good, the consequences will be minimized. The requirements are that there be immediate notification of the release, remedial measures be undertaken, dangerous goods being transported be marked with identification labels and placards, and that shipping documents clearly identify the dangerous goods, thereby providing immediate information to emergency response personnel.
In addition, for certain more dangerous goods, the regulations require that before shipment occurs, the shipper have in place an emergency response assistance plan detailing how the shipper will respond to correct the effects of any accidental release.
To further support emergency response measures, Transport Canada produced a book entitled Guide to Initial Emergency Response. This has received wide distribution in Canada. It provides advice on initial actions to be taken in the event of an accidental release.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It pertains to the crisis in China.

security.

Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that I made the point yesterday that in a country of the power and size of China the disorder that is occurring cannot long remain an internal matter. However, I know that all Members of the House of Commons would want the United Nations to respect the letter of its charter, and

June 7, 1989
Oral Questions
that they would also want the Government of Canada to respect the charter.
Today, the Prime Minister has signed a letter to the Secretary General of the United Nations which does two things. First, it conveys to the Secretary General the resolution adopted unanimously by the House of Commons on Monday night and the record of debate.
It also indicates to the Secretary General that Canada would support very strongly both his leadership and action that might be taken through ECOSOC and action that might be taken through the Human Rights Commission. subtopic: EVACUATION PLANS FOR CANADIANS IN CHINA
EVACUATION PLANS FOR CANADIANS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this morning's news reports we heard that an emergency evacuation of American Embassy staff and dependants was unsuccessful and that they were still trapped in the compound. We have also heard that the Army is getting ready to move against students on university campuses around China.
I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs how many Canadians are still trapped in Beijing. What is being done to evacuate those Canadians who are still in other Chinese cities and on other university campuses that are not in the vicinity of Beijing or Shanghai?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EVACUATION PLANS FOR CANADIANS IN CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House would be pleased to know that a chartered Canadian Airlines International DC-10 left Beijing with 251 Canadian passengers last night. It has arrived safely in Tokyo.
There would be in the neighbourhood of 30 to 40 Canadians remaining in Beijing. Some of those are Canadian Embassy officials. They will be remaining there for the foreseeable future to maintain Canadian activities there.
I have issued an advisory to Canadians elsewhere in China that it is the view of the Government that it would be wise for them to leave other parts of China. We are putting in place arrangements that will help them move out.
There are some complications that I should draw to the attention of the House. One is that some Canadians are in particularly remote parts of China. Jet aircraft cannot land in some of those locations. We are looking into the chartering of smaller aircraft that might be able to get into those more remote areas.
These are problems which are not faced by Canada alone. Other countries involved, such as the United States, as the Hon. Member mentioned, Australia, the U.K., and others are facing similar difficulties. We are pooling our resources.
For example, we have made an arrangement with Australia by which vacant spaces on one of its planes coming out of Beijing and Shanghai tomorrow will be made available to Canadians. In exchange we will make available to Australians and to others vacant spaces on another chartered Canadian Airlines flight that will be leaving Beijing and Shanghai on Friday.
We believe we have identified the location of Canadians throughout China. There are some technical problems in ensuring that we can get to all of them as quickly as we would like to, but in working with other countries we are doing our best.

To quote the Minister, he said: "For instance, you take China. Some people are putting China forward as a potential area for sales. Obviously the NPT becomes an issue."
June 7, 1989

Will the Minister today renounce the dangerous policy review that he has undertaken, especially in light of the recent events in China? Does the Minister not recognize that Canada's participation in the non-proliferation treaty is crucial?

At no time did I refer to the NPT to say that I am reviewing it, that we want to change it, or that we will lessen it.
When I referred to China and the NPT, obviously until China signs the NPT specifically for CANDU reactors or any other nuclear technology Canada could not co-operate.

Mr. Speaker, the direct quote is still on tape. The Minister and nobody else but the Minister raised the issue of the sale of a nuclear reactor to China. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege of tabling in the House of Commons the Vienna closing document which was recently accepted by the 35 countries which took part in the Conference on Co-operation and Security in Europe.

In the Government's view, this Vienna concluding document represents an historic milestone in the process of the Conference on Co-operation and Security in Europe. The document contains new and expanded commitments in the fields of military security, human rights and contacts, and humanitarian and economic
co-operation. Taken together, these Vienna provisions, for which Canada negotiated hard, and to which Canada is firmly committed, will help to move the European and North American states toward greater levels of mutual security and co-operation.

Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has already presented the Vienna concluding document to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade. By tabling this agreement in the House today, the Government reaffirms Canada's will to enlighten as many of its citizens as possible about the Conference's proceedings and the Vienna concluding document.

The House resumed from Tuesday, June 6, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall: That Bill C-21, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Employment and Immigration Department and Commission Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Allmand (p. 2685).

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part, on behalf of the Government, in the debate on second reading of Bill C-21 amending the Unemployment Insurance Act.
This Bill is of great importance for the future of our country and for working men and women. It shows once again our Government's determination to help workers adjust to technological changes and meet competition in the next decade. While their prosperity depends on a healthy economy, it also depends on their ability and their productivity.
In the 1990s, working men and women will operate in a much more complex world where microelectronics, telecommunications, robotics and automation will impinge on all trades and professions. The pressures of competition, technological change and the demands of the market will thoroughly change the structure of the labour market in Canada and mean that there will be fewer and fewer positions for workers with little education and training.
Already, Mr. Speaker, more than a million workers have difficulty finding work because they lack skills. This trend is expected to increase because of certain demographic factors. In the 1970s, the labour force grew by about 300,000 annually, but the number of workers is expected to grow by only 180,000 (annually) in the 1990s. Statistics Canada reports that 14 per cent of Canadian
manufacturers already have production difficulties due to a lack of skilled labour.
Mr. Speaker, we must always keep in mind the background for this reform: workers want to work and to have steady jobs in which they can fulfill themselves as human beings.
Too many workers are still caught in the vicious circle of odd jobs, unemployment insurance or welfare, which we must break.
In Canada, Mr. Speaker, we spend $12 billion a year on unemployment insurance benefits and only $400 million on training for workers. Our countiy is falling behind other industrial powers with respect to worker training and retraining.
The strategy we are proposing to Canadians, Mr. Speaker, is to change the present use of unemployment insurance funds and reallocate them to train UI recipients, while of course preserving the income safety net unemployment insurance represents for all workers.
Mr. Speaker, the changes are intended to make the Unemployment Insurance Program an active program. Why spend $12 billion to keep people at home? In fact, one of Quebec's greatest poets, Felix Leclerc, said that the best way to kill a man was to pay him to do nothing.
Whatever our friends opposite seem to think, we are not saving any money. Twelve billion dollars will be spent, except that a larger part will go to training, to give additional tools to those who want to meet the challenges of the 1990s. The level of assistance has been definitely enhanced.
The reform would not be worth the paper it was written on if the Government cannot depend on the support of all its economic partners, especially the private sector, which will be asked to play a far more important role. Job training is above all the responsibility of employers and employees, and in the present situation, the private sector must be a more active force. It is in their own interests and those of their employees, whose skills and productivity are essential if businesses are to be competitive.
Today, Canadian businesses are not working hard enough on occupational training. This must improve, Mr. Speaker. It is true that we as a government intend to inject $230 million into increasing training activities in the private sector through co-operative programs. The private sector will be urged in turn to invest its share of funds in training. The National Skills Development Advisory Board which the Government intends to estab-
June 7, 1989

lish will provide the Government with guidance on the needs of the private sector.
The $230 million designated for the private sector breaks down as follows: $65 million will be spent on sectoral human resources planning; $100 million will be spent on developing the skills of young Canadians who do not have the qualifications for today's jobs and need help to make the transition from school to work; $15 million will be used to provide more assistance to businesses in adjusting their labour force when they are either expanding, shutting down or introducing technological change; $50 million will be used to help 200 designated communities whose economic situation has been affected by market developments. This amount is in addition to the $148 million already earmarked by the Government for job creation.
All these measures, Mr. Speaker, not only infuse our training programs with greater vigour, they are also adapted to the situation in disadvantaged regions.
The Unemployment Insurance Program will not only be more active, it will also play a development role. That is what I call making the most of our resources for the common good!
At this point, I think we should remember that having a job means a lot more than getting a pay cheque every week. It also means feeling that one is participating fully in the economic growth of our society. When someone is unemployed and finally gets a job, that very fact often means restored dignity and self-esteem and, especially, a chance to realize, to explore potential that would have been wasted.
In addition, the Government will be providing an additional $50 million to the $50 million already available under the Canada Assistance Plan, in order to help social assistance recipients acquire the skills and experience they need to get a job.
This particular group consists of a large number of young people between the ages of 18 and 25. As someone who has worked for many years in education and business, I find it particularly sad that one young person out of three is unable to finish high school. We must pay special attention to these young people who constitute a tremendous resource for our society. If we fail to act quickly to bring a large number of the 18 to 25 group into the labour force, we run the risk of excluding
Unemployment Insurance Act
them forever from the mainstream of society, with all the social costs that implies.
Together with provincial funds, more than $200 million more will be spent annually on re-employment of social assistance recipients. In concrete terms, 20,000 recipients will have a chance to upgrade their training. Considering the extent of the federal Government's contribution, it is obviously false to claim that the legislation's new provisions would have the effect of increasing the number of social assistance recipients, and thus increase the financial burden on the provinces. We must not forget that first of all, under the Canada Assistance Plan the federal Government is responsible for funding half the costs of social assistance, and second, that the training and re-employment programs proposed under the new strategy will reduce the number of welfare recipients.
The Government also believes that more must be done to improve the situation of unemployed older workers. One hundred million dollars will be provided to cover the costs of hiring and training workers laid off as a result of changes in technology and demand.
Other incentives for this kind of worker to find another job quickly are also planned. These will be in addition to those already provided by existing Jobs Strategy programs.
The Bill submitted for the approval of the House, Mr. Speaker, thoroughly changes the present special benefits plan.
In order to meet the requirements of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, our Government intends not only to guarantee parental benefits for natural and adoptive parents but also to make the special benefits provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act more flexible. Under the new provisions, both parents will be able to share 10 weeks of benefits after the birth or adoption of a child. The new plan will allow beneficiaries to combine sickness, maternity and parental benefits up to the maximum allowable, 30 weeks.
The combination of maternity and sickness benefits, now limited to 145 weeks, will therefore be eliminated. These new provisions will cost the Unemployment Insurance Plan another $450 million. This is, Mr. Speaker, a beautiful example of a Government that is concerned with the condition of women and young couples and that is not afraid to act in a tangible way to enable them to

June 7, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
reconcile their carreer objectives with their parental responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, I consider that all forms of discrimination towards older people must disappear. I am happy that this bill allows people who are 65 years of age or more to be treated as full citizens. Older people will be able to contribute to the unemployment insurance system and to take advantage of all its benefits. These new provisions which will cost $40 million are not only in keeping with the Charter of Rights but they recognize the privilege of Canadian men and women who are 65 or more to retire later. We must recognize that senior citizens have the inalienable right to decide for themselves.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the Bill has other provisions whose goal is to eliminate some unfair restrictions on eligibility to benefits during work action.
Presently, Mr. Speaker, the legislation does not allow the paying of benefits for sickness or maternity during work action. We think that this an inequitable and retrograde provision that this House would like to do away with.
It would have certainly been easier to leave things the way they were by simply bringing in some minor amendments for window dressing and thus being seen as doing much while doing very little actually.
Bill C-21 and the Labour Force Development Strategy are not just a masking exercise. They go straight to the source of the problem, that is to give Canada a skilled labour force capable of facing up to the challenges that the 21st century will bring.
Our goal is to preserve the important role of Unemployment Insurance as an income maintenance program, while eliminating elements that encourage inactivity, especially in areas where the economy is strong.
To respect regional differences, we have also taken into account regions like mine, Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup, where the unemployment rate is high.
In addition to training programs, Mr. Speaker, these regions will get special assistance for community development as well as measures supporting local entrepreneurship.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, all that has been done while taking into account the differences between Canadian regions, despite those who would like us to treat all parts of Canada as one and the same.
In brief, in regions where there are more available jobs, people will have to work a greater number of weeks to be eligible for benefits and their benefit period will be shorter. Conversely, in regions with high unemployment rates, workers won't be affected by those measures, Mr. Speaker.
As a Government, we fully recognize the vital role played by the unemployment insurance system as a social safety net and we have no intention to undermine it. On the contrary! However, we are aware that the present system has shortcomings and doesn't offer any alternative. Bill C-21 proposes alternatives, Mr. Speaker. The risk was high but my Government has made a commitment to improve the lot of the unemployed, not to please unions, employers or the electorate but to assume its responsibilities, and that is what we have done.
All the changes proposed in Bill C-21 have essentially been designed to make that system more efficient and equitable and to meet the needs of workers. Like any Government measure, Mr. Speaker, this Bill imposes restrictions and obligations. As legislators, we have to look beyond the selective disadvantages which so often arise from the measures that we are taking. We must look at the potential long-term advantages of these measures, certainly for the people concerned, but also for the collectivity as a whole.
M. Speaker, Bill C-21, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, is a legislative measure which will be beneficial for workers as a whole. Once again, its purpose is to give additional tools and a hope for a better future to thousands of Canadiens presently unemployed. Having valued for a long time leisure, physical fitness or consumption, the time has come to value work. That is what this Bill does.
For all those reasons, M. Speaker, I would urge my colleagues to support this Bill.
June 7, 1989

speechtext: On questions or comments, the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity- Conception.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to what the Hon. Member for Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup had to say and I did find it very interesting.
There are certain aspects of this proposed amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act which I would certainly like to bring to the attention of the House and on which I would certainly like to make some comments. I have spent the last couple of weeks dealing with an upset that one aspect of this amendment has caused in my riding.
I would like to read the press release of the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration dated June 1, 1989. In part it reads, and I am quoting verbatim:
The legislation, part of the government's recently announced Labour Force Development Strategy "Success in Works", strengthens the ability of the UI program to continue to act as an economic safety net by focusing on those in need.
There is an aspect of this legislation which has impinged on my riding in a very unsatisfactory, devastating, and disconcerting manner. I speak now of one particular aspect with which I am sure many Members certainly on this side of the House are very familiar. I am talking about the job development strategywhich has been put in place. I speak not only for my riding, but I am sure I speak for the other ridings in Newfoundland, and certainly for other parts of Atlantic Canada because it was discussed this morning at various meetings.
The whole problem with this business is that the job development strategy has been a benefit to my riding not only as a safety net for insurable earnings under UI but as part of the community development programs. I have ten rural development committees in my riding. They have all been absolutely devastated by the abruptness of this change.
It was quoted in the press release that this change will have the program continue to act as an economic safety net. I am in receipt of a letter to one of my constituents. I wish to quote from part of it. It involves a job development application. There are hundreds of these letters in
Unemployment Insurance Act
my riding right now. The contents of it have been sent without consultation with me, without consultation with the rural development associations and their committees, and without consultation with any of the leaders of the community. I am talking about 260 communities in my riding. Your Honour can imagine why my office and my constituency assistant are inundated with telephone calls. We do not have enough people to man the two lines that we have. The letter states in part:
Your application for funding under the Job Development Program has been assessed.
The Job Development Program is not designed to be a safety net which provides insurable employment, or a mechanism which provides community infrastructure and nothing else. The objective of Job Development is to assist long-term unemployed individuals by providing them with training and work experience in occupations with real potential for employment.
Your application is not being recommended as the training is for occupations that are either surplus to the labour market or are not in demand.
I live in a riding that is essentially a one industry riding. The transfer of $800 million for training does not make a lot of sense to me. That equates to $30 million that will not be used for unemployed people in Newfoundland. A great deal of it will pertain to my riding.
When people call me up, what do I explain to them? I say: "Yes, this was meant, I believe, for retraining programs." Retraining is fine in Toronto, Oshawa, or any other of the urban communities where there is not one industry but 50 or maybe 100 such as sheet metal works, fabricating companies, car factories, and ship building factories. There is no ship building in Bonavista, Newfoundland. There is no sheet metal works in Clarenville. None of these things exist. We have the potential for job training, but where are the jobs? I do not know what I can tell my constituents when they call. I do not know what I should say. Should I say: "Go back and submit a project where you have a strong element of job training"? They will ask me: "What kind of job training, trained to do what kind of jobs?"
I do not want to become repetitive, but I hope many of my constituents watching this debate. I hope that in the next three or four days or the next week or so, as long as we can talk about Bill C-21, that as a minimum they will have a better understanding for what the Government is trying to do. I do not understand it. I certainly cannot support it. I have to speak up for what might have been a well intentioned macro change for the country, but

June 7, 1989
Unemployment Insurance Act
which certainly does not pertain to my riding. I suggest that it does not pertain to many other rural ridings in Canada.
It grieves me to no end that on the one hand the Minister for International Trade says that Newfoundland is going to get $15 million moreand on the other hand the Minister of Employment and Immigration comes out with a document in which the result is that we are going to get $30 million less; $30 million minus and $15 million plus still gives me a minus $15 million.
I want to go on record to acknowledge that I am going to do as much in my power as I can to ensure that the Canadian public is aware of the inconsistencies. I will do my utmost to make the people of Canada aware that these letters have been going out to well intentioned people who are expecting something for their communities, something for their unemployment insurance, something to boost their earnings. They get nothing but a cold letter indicating that there has been an abrupt, terrible and disconcerting change.
As their Member of Parliament, unfortunately I have to say to them: "I have not been consulted. I have not been briefed. I have not been made aware of these changes for which I have to answer to you and to the people of my riding."
I suggest that there are many other people certainly on this side of the House, and I would suggest on the other side of the House although they may not want to admit it, who are in exactly the same position.
I beg your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, to allow me to wrap up this by saying that I wish there were some other way that we could look at this.
I wish that the Minister of Employment and Immigration as a minimum would have a look at the concerns of Atlantic Canada and the rural ridings to see if there is something positive that can be done so that we can slow down this abruptness. I hope that there will and can be some amelioration of this job development program as a minimum to allow us more flexibility in those areas. It does not matter what we train people to do if there are no jobs for areas in which there can be no industry.
